We reflect upon the past research related to the network security of IT/IoT/OT devices, conducted by us and other researchers. We provide recommendations to asset owners on getting started with independent security evaluations of these devices. Presentation Material • Download Slides

sessions.title: 0Work: Sandbox-to-Host Escape Chain in Claude Cowork
sessions.abstract: 0Work: Sandbox-to-Host Escape Chain in Claude Cowork Vladimir Tokarev | Vulnerability Reserach Tech Lead, Cyera Fufu Shpigelman | AI Security Researcher, Cyera Ofek Itach | Security Research Team Lead, Cyera Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD Claude Cowork is Anthropic's autonomous AI agent for enterprise knowledge work. It runs inside an isolated Linux VM on the user's machine, connected to 278+ MCP integrations (Slack, GitHub, Gmail, Stripe, Google Drive), and handles code execution to file processing for 245 million monthly active users across Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. 70% of Fortune 100 companies are Claude customers. The VM is the security boundary. Malicious code can run inside it, crash it, wipe it, and none of that reaches the host. We will present a full guest-to-host escape chain, validated in production, starting from a malicious npm package, poisoned GitHub repo, or prompt injection. The chain crosses eight security boundaries: Cowork's npm --ignore-scripts defense fails to stop the package install lifecycle in the production sandbox; CVE-2026-43284 (Dirty Frag) gives kernel root; root enables extraction of the MITM proxy's ECDSA P256 CA private key from the Go heap via a novel pointer-chase; with the key we replace the TLS proxy and inject fabricated tool calls into API responses; the host trusts the injected calls and dispatches them to MCP connectors running outside the VM. In bypassPermissions mode or during unattended Routines, this yields 0-click host code execution. Outside those modes, a 1-click path (.terminal present_files) still reaches the host. Once on the host, the stolen OAuth token enables cascading access into connected services: Slack, GitHub, Google Workspace, and Stripe through the MCP connector architecture. Attendees leave with the full technical chain (kernel to crypto to protocol to host), reusable audit methodology for AI agent sandboxes, and defensive patterns for "tool injection" against agentic systems. Takeaway All host-to-API traffic routes through the VM, and the signing key is in memory: Cowork's architecture sends every API request from the host through a TLS-intercepting proxy inside the VM. The proxy's ECDSA private key sits in the sdk-daemon process heap. An attacker with root in that VM can extract the key and gain full visibility into, and control over, every interaction between the user and the model. Attendees can audit whether their own agent deployments expose signing material inside the execution sandbox. Supply chain is the natural entry point for agent exploitation: Cowork relies on npm --ignore-scripts as a defense, but in the production sandbox a package install lifecycle script still executes and delivers attacker code. AI agents install packages without second-guessing them; obfuscated payloads (zlib + base64) bypass the model's code inspection. Attendees can block all lifecycle scripts at the package manager level and detect compressed/encoded payloads in CI/CD and agent environments. Root in the VM collapses all remaining boundaries at once: there is no defense-in-depth between "kernel root inside the sandbox" and "full host control." Once root is achieved, credential theft, CA key extraction, proxy replacement, and API response injection all follow without any additional exploit. Attendees should evaluate whether their agent sandboxes have independent security layers that survive a kernel compromise.

sessions.title: Bad Connection: Global Telecom Exploitation by Covert Surveillance Actors
sessions.abstract: Bad Connection: Global Telecom Exploitation by Covert Surveillance Actors Swantje Lange | PhD Candidate, Hasso Plattner Institute, University of Potsdam & The Citizen Lab Fellow Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Mobile, Network Security Vault Recording: TBD Location tracking campaigns are an ongoing issue in the telecom ecosystem. Surveillance actors with access to the interconnect backbone can stealthily conduct attacks that often remain undetected for years. Analyzing network telemetry, we were for the first time able to map real-world attack traffic to mobile operator signaling infrastructure. After a brief introduction to the (lack of) security of the telecom signaling ecosystem, we will present how attackers gain access to the system and misuse it for location-tracking attempts. We will detail our approach, showing how we identified two different actors allegedly running commercial surveillance platforms supporting state-sponsored intelligence activities. We will provide insight into the actors' operations, highlighting their attack patterns and mechanics. Takeaway Location-tracking attacks in the telecom ecosystem are still widespread in 2026. Enforceable interconnect controls, transparency in commercial network access, and regulatory accountability are essential to restrain the surveillance activities. Attendees learn how mobile network operators can detect such attacks, and understand common mitigations and why they are ineffective.

sessions.title: Bad Coworker: Turning Microsoft Cowork Into a Cross-Tenant Backdoor
sessions.abstract: Bad Coworker: Turning Microsoft Cowork Into a Cross-Tenant Backdoor Ben Zamir | Security Research, Cymulate Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Enterprise AI agents are no longer simple chat interfaces. They impersonate users, execute code inside isolated containers, process sensitive organizational data and maintain persistent workspaces. These capabilities create new security boundaries and risks. This research presents three vulnerabilities in Microsoft Cowork that was recently released, completely break those boundaries at different layers, demonstrating the new AI era risks. A critical cross-tenant vulnerability allowed an external attacker to reach the Cowork orchestration control plane and take control of a victim's live AI workspace, a local privilege escalation allowed code executing with root access inside the Cowork container and an authorization vulnerability exposed other users' private AI conversation data, including prompts, responses, tool activity and data processed by the agent. The Briefing also introduces a new method for remotely researching an isolated AI workspace through a unique command channel. By using legitimate Cowork file synchronization behavior, an external operator could exchange tasks and results with the container, combine local execution with LLM assistance and remotely control and research from both inside and outside the isolated environment. Together, the findings demonstrate how failures in container, control-plane and MCP utilization can transform an enterprise AI assistant into a backdoor remotely controlled interface to identities, data, applications and Microsoft services. Takeaway Understand the security boundaries of modern enterprise AI workspaces. Attendees will learn how container isolation, orchestration gateways, cloud identity, conversation storage and connected AI tools combine to form the security model of an enterprise agent such as Microsoft Cowork. Recognize how a compromise inside an AI workspace can extend beyond the application. Attendees will understand how root access, control-plane authentication failures and connected Microsoft 365 tools can turn a container-level issue into session hijacking, identity abuse, sensitive-data access and control of enterprise applications. Assess and harden AI agent isolation across container, control-plane and data layers. Attendees will understand modern Cowork agents and their privilege boundaries, service-to-service authentication, tenant isolation, conversation authorization, file-based communication channels and the permissions exposed through agent tools.

sessions.title: Behind the Response: Technical Lessons from Real National Cyber Incident Response
sessions.abstract: Behind the Response: Technical Lessons from Real National Cyber Incident Response Esmeralda Kazia | Chief Technology Officer (OT, ICS & Automation), Albanian Power Corporation (KESH) Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Defense & Resilience, Enterprise Security Vault Recording: TBD Every major cyber incident begins with uncertainty. Alerts are incomplete, telemetry is fragmented, threat intelligence is often contradictory, and critical decisions cannot wait. This Briefing takes attendees inside the technical reality of responding to large-scale cyber incidents affecting government organizations and critical infrastructure. Rather than presenting another incident response framework or theoretical playbook, this Briefing examines what actually happens when defenders face sophisticated adversaries operating in real environments. Through carefully anonymized operational case studies, the Briefing explores how incident responders validate incomplete evidence, build investigative hypotheses, adapt detection logic during active operations, integrate threat intelligence into tactical decision-making, and coordinate response while services remain under pressure. The presentation focuses on the practical challenges that rarely appear in incident response documentation: evolving attacker behavior, changing priorities, incomplete visibility, detection failures, and the continuous adjustments required to maintain operational awareness. Attendees will also see how threat hunting, detection engineering, and intelligence-driven analysis become dynamic processes during active incidents rather than predefined procedures. The Briefing concludes with a practical operational methodology that organizations can adopt to improve decision-making, detection maturity, and cyber resilience during high-pressure incidents. All examples are derived from real operational experience and have been fully anonymized to protect sensitive information while preserving the technical lessons that matter most. Takeaway Build adaptive incident response workflows that remain effective when traditional playbooks no longer match the reality of an ongoing attack. Improve detection engineering and threat hunting by integrating threat intelligence, behavioral analysis, and continuous hypothesis validation during live operations. Apply a practical operational methodology for making faster, better-informed technical decisions under uncertainty while responding to complex cyber incidents.

sessions.title: Below the Model: Least-Privilege Containment for Autonomous Browser Agents in Chromium
sessions.abstract: Below the Model: Least-Privilege Containment for Autonomous Browser Agents in Chromium Ariel Koren | Innovation Elad Mintzer | Innovation Shlomi Azoulay | Machine Learning Engineer and Security Researcher, Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Defense, AI & ML: Attack and Defense Vault Recording: TBD An agent shopping for earbuds reads a product review that tells it to add a protection plan first. It obeys, and the cart lands 34 percent over the user's hard cap. Nothing malfunctioned. A language model cannot reliably separate the user's instructions from attacker-controlled page text, because both arrive as tokens inside the same reasoning context. Once the model is hijacked, the browser still gives the agent the user's full authority. This research takes the opposite route from model-side hardening. Instead of asking the model to behave, it moves enforcement below the model and into Chromium. Every browser-driving agent ultimately speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so the browser turns that dispatch point into a deterministic least-privilege chokepoint. Each automation client receives a transport-derived identity the model cannot spoof. Hundreds of protocol commands collapse into a small set of semantic action types. Every action receives an allow, block, or native human-confirmation verdict. The agent also declares, per subtask, which origins and action classes it needs. The browser enforces the intersection between that declaration and the baseline policy. A declaration can only narrow authority, never widen it. Off-scope origins receive an empty ephemeral cookie jar through partial-incognito routing, so a shopping task cannot read the user's inbox or steal unrelated session credentials. The Briefing demonstrates three live browser-agent hijacks, then shows each one contained by browser-side enforcement. The model reasons. The browser decides. Takeaway A practical architecture for placing the AI-agent security boundary below the model. The Chrome DevTools Protocol dispatch point becomes a least-privilege chokepoint that a compromised agent cannot route around, while client identity is derived from transport state rather than model text. A threat model for browser-agent hijack as runtime drift. The Briefing separates four concrete drift classes discovered through live attacks: context drift, origin drift, cookie-session drift, and budget drift. Each class maps to a browser-side enforcement point that teams can test against their own agents. A deployable credential-isolation primitive for agentic browsing: partial incognito. In-scope origins receive the user's real cookies, autofill, and permissions. Off-scope origins receive an empty ephemeral jar inside the same browsing task. There is no URL blocklist to maintain, and unrelated session credentials are not exposed to the agent.

sessions.title: Breaking Android's Last Recovery Boundary: From Malicious APK Resources to Zero-Click MMS PDoS
sessions.abstract: Breaking Android's Last Recovery Boundary: From Malicious APK Resources to Zero-Click MMS PDoS AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Sheng (Cxxsheng) Cao | PhD Candidate, Huazhong University of Science and Technology Zhiniang Peng | Associate Professor, Huazhong University of Science and Technology Songzhou (Canyie) Shi | Security Researcher, LSPosed Team Haoyu Wang | Professor, Huazhong University of Science and Technology Hao Zhou | Research Assistant Professor, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University WeiMin Cheng | Independent Researcher Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Mobile, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Android packages treat manifests, XML metadata, strings, drawables, and images as static resources, yet privileged framework components routinely parse those resources during service startup and security-sensitive UI flows. A manifest may store only a compact resource ID while AAPT places the referenced value in Binary XML, resources.arsc, a compressed APK entry, or an image file. Package Manager records the component at installation, but a later system-service lifecycle becomes the parser of the package-owned bytes. Our first proof used this separation to inject an enormous UTF-16 value through Account Manager. The crash was reproduced but rejected as a security issue because Safe Mode could remove the third-party package. That rejection changed the research question: does Safe Mode actually prevent every privileged lifecycle from resolving attacker-controlled resources? It does not. We found direct Package Manager lookups that bypass Safe Mode's intent-resolution filter (C1), boot-time metadata queries that execute before the filter becomes active (C2), and a Device Admin revocation deadlock in which the only removal UI parses resources owned by the admin it must remove. We also reconstructed a complementary remote path: a crafted DNG received by the preinstalled messaging application is rendered by SystemUI as notification content, replayed after SystemUI restarts, and rebuilt from persistent message state after reboot. Safe Mode keeps both privileged components enabled, so a trusted package identity continues to replay attacker-controlled media. Framework-realistic fuzzing supplied the XML, drawable, and native-image failure primitives used to exercise these recovery paths. We use recovery-resistant PDoS to mean that ordinary reboot, Safe Mode, and normal role-removal or uninstall flows do not restore a usable device. Factory reset remains effective, and privileged ADB or recovery intervention may also recover a suitably configured device. The campaign produced 33 tracked reports, 12 rated Critical and 15 rated High, which were assigned 18 Android CVEs. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Attendees will come away understanding how Android's consumer recovery protections are actually supposed to work, Safe Mode's package-level filtering, the intent-resolution gate that is meant to enforce it, and the role-revocation flow meant to let a user remove a privileged app, and exactly where each of those protections quietly stops applying: an API that never enters the filtering path, a boot window before the filter is active, and an identity-based exemption that never checks what content a trusted app is allowed to keep processing. Attendees will see a concrete technique for converting a parser crash into an unremovable privileged state: when the only UI that can revoke a role must render that role owner's resources before exposing the revoke control, crashing that UI leaves the role permanently active, no different in practical effect from a privilege the user can no longer take back. Attendees will see every denial-of-service category Android's own disclosure process recognizes, demonstrated end to end in a single campaign: locally

sessions.title: Breaking Kerberos Trust Boundaries: From On-Demand Relay to Hybrid Identity Compromise
sessions.abstract: Breaking Kerberos Trust Boundaries: From On-Demand Relay to Hybrid Identity Compromise Ben Zamir | Security Research, Cymulate Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Enterprise Security, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD As Microsoft moves toward disabling NTLM, many organizations expect practical authentication relay attacks to disappear. This research demonstrates the opposite: relay is evolving into a Kerberos-native attack class with impact across enterprise services, protected HTTPS endpoints, and hybrid cloud identity. This Briefing presents four previously unknown Kerberos relay findings, each independently recognized by Microsoft. CVE-2026-20929 introduces on-demand Kerberos relay through DNS CNAME abuse, allowing authentication to be generated for attacker-selected services. A separate DNS-independent relay primitive removes a major operational limitation of earlier techniques and led to the discovery of a critical vulnerability in a Microsoft service that lacked effective relay enforcement. The research also uncovers a vulnerability in a hybrid Azure identity workflow that allows relayed on-premises authentication to cross a trust boundary and compromise a cloud identity. Finally, the research uncovers a Windows HTTP Negotiate vulnerability that bypasses Extended Protection for Authentication and Channel Binding Token protections over HTTPS, challenging the primary defenses against authentication relay. Together, these findings show that Kerberos relay is not a narrow successor to NTLM relay, but a broader and more consequential attack surface spanning service authentication, transport protections and hybrid identity trust. This Briefing will present the protocol research, end-to-end attack chains, demonstrations, tooling and defensive guidance needed to reassess Kerberos relay exposure. Takeaway Understand how Kerberos authentication behaves in modern, hardened enterprise environments. Attendees will learn how Kerberos relay remains relevant after NTLM reduction, including against services protected by Extended Protection for Authentication and Channel Binding Tokens. Recognize how Kerberos relay risk changes in hybrid identity environments. Attendees will understand how authentication originating in on-premises Active Directory can interact with cloud identity workflows and how failures in those trust relationships can allow relay impact to extend beyond the local domain, including MFA relationships. Assess Kerberos relay exposure across services, endpoints and identity boundaries. Attendees will leave with a practical framework for reviewing Kerberos-enabled services, testing assumptions around EPA and Channel Binding Tokens, identifying unexpected relay targets and prioritizing detection, hardening and patching.

sessions.title: By Any Means Necessary: How Rogue AI Swarms Abuse Public Infrastructure to Bypass Sandbox Restrictions
sessions.abstract: By Any Means Necessary: How Rogue AI Swarms Abuse Public Infrastructure to Bypass Sandbox Restrictions Tamir Ishay Sharbat | Director of Security Research, Zenity Avishai Efrat | Senior Security Researcher, Zenity Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Threat Hunting & Incident Response, AI & ML: Attack and Defense Vault Recording: TBD We discovered thousands of unreported messages from rogue AI agent swarms hidden somewhere nobody was looking: inside URLs. These messages reveal how agents encoded HTML and Javascript into addresses on public httpbin-like services and abused public infrastructure to increase their network reach and complete their tasks. This Briefing focuses on the chains created by the agents, and the techniques behind those chains. We show how these messages uncover the swarm's circumvention methods and how the agents built a URL laundering mechanism for broader network access, chaining dozens of ordinary public services that their sandboxes allowed in order to access restricted destinations. Agents ran Javascript by hijacking online scanning services which have remote browsing capabilities, encoding scripts with elaborate functionality and abusing the services' infrastructure to get to otherwise inaccessible targets. Here, the URL laundering moves into Javascript fetch calls, placing the requests well outside the agents' original sandbox controls. The controls most organizations rely on today for network sandboxing, such as host-based allowlists and HTTP request method restrictions, are exactly the ones these techniques bypass. Building on these concepts, we elaborate on what's required to identify rogue agents attacking your infrastructure, as well as on how to detect and restrict misaligned AI when running your own agents. Takeaway Agents are determined to achieve their goal at whatever means possible. They are consistently finding creative and sophisticated ways to bypass their restrictions, coordinate with other agents and cross into systems unrelated to their initial goals. Defenders need to start considering their next attacker might be an agent, on a different assignment, using your infra as a stepping stone. Naive egress controls won't hold swarms back. Swarms circumvent these controls by chaining encoders, redirectors, fetchers, remote browsing execution and any available service that extends their capability. This is a bigger lesson, we need to start thinking about more durable ways to contain agents. As they become more capable of finding paths around restrictions, the boundaries we put in place must hold even when our own agents push against them. Protecting your infrastructure from rogue AI agents' abuse requires anticipating future swarm patterns and capabilities that misaligned AI will seek. This means both understanding current observed attacks vectors, as well as considering what these could evolve to become in the future.

sessions.title: Cache&Release: Turning Artifact Repositories into an Organization Wide Supply Chain Attack
sessions.abstract: Cache&Release: Turning Artifact Repositories into an Organization Wide Supply Chain Attack Uri Katz | Director of Research, OLIGO Security Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery, AI & ML: Attack and Defense Vault Recording: TBD Modern software development depends on internal artifact repositories to store, cache, and distribute software across the enterprise. Developers, CI/CD pipelines, and increasingly AI agents all trust these systems as the source of the code they execute. In this talk, we will demonstrate how that trust can be turned against itself. We will present, for the first time, the full technical details behind a flaw that enables attacks against artifact repositories that allows a single request to poison a shared cache and transparently redirect future package downloads to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Every subsequent consumer receives malicious code while believing it originated from a trusted internal repository. This will include demonstrations of the complete attack chain the vulnerability enables, showing how compromising the software distribution layer enables malicious code to propagate across development environments without targeting individual endpoints. As AI agents increasingly resolve dependencies, install packages, and execute code autonomously, the impact extends beyond traditional software supply chain attacks. The same trusted repository now serves both humans and autonomous systems, creating a shared point of compromise capable of influencing software execution at organizational scale. Takeaway Scrutinize your artifact manager the same as any other component of your threat model. Verify package integrity independently of where it was served from. Recognize that security controls can become attack surfaces themselves.

sessions.title: CADScanner: Breaking Open Compiled AutoCAD Malware - Recovering FAS and VLX for Industrial Threat Analysis
sessions.abstract: CADScanner: Breaking Open Compiled AutoCAD Malware - Recovering FAS and VLX for Industrial Threat Analysis Chenghui Liang | Senior Security Engineer, Sangfor Technologies Inc. Xiaotian Wang | Undergraduate Student, Lanzhou University Luxing Yin | PhD Candidate, Lanzhou University Chang Sun | Undergraduate Student, Lanzhou University Qingguo Zhou | Professor, Lanzhou University Xin Liu | Associate Professor, Lanzhou University Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Malware Vault Recording: TBD Engineering organizations routinely exchange AutoCAD drawings across internal teams, contractors, and suppliers. Less visible is the executable ecosystem that travels with those drawings: AutoLISP scripts and their compiled FAS and VLX forms. These compiled formats have been used in documented industrial espionage campaigns, yet they remain largely opaque to defenders. Cloud sandboxing is often prohibited for proprietary CAD data, public AutoCAD malware tooling focuses on plaintext LSP, and encrypted FAS/VLX artifacts are routinely skipped during triage. This Briefing presents our research into recovering and analyzing compiled AutoCAD malware. We reverse engineered the FAS4 binary format, including its dual encrypted streams and rolling XOR recovery process, and reconstructed the VLX VRTLIB-1 container format used to package multiple AutoCAD modules. We then show how recovered symbols, APIs, strings, paths, registry references, and structural metadata can be lifted into a security-oriented intermediate representation suitable for behavioral analysis and ATT&CK-mapped evidence. Our evaluation on a 983-sample corpus spanning 23 malware families shows that format recovery is the missing layer: before recovery, plaintext rules and raw string matching provide almost no visibility into encrypted FAS samples; after recovery, security-relevant indicators become available for practical detection. The resulting analysis reaches 95.8% TPR at 2.2% FPR on family-disjoint local detection, with per-file processing under 15 ms. Attendees will learn how compiled AutoCAD malware works, how FAS and VLX can be recovered, and how this approach generalizes to proprietary industrial formats where defenders lack analyzable input. Takeaway Compiled AutoCAD malware is primarily a visibility problem: encrypted FAS files and containerized VLX archives hide behavior that plaintext rules, raw string scanning, and routine SOC workflows cannot reliably inspect. FAS4 and VLX recovery turns opaque CAD artifacts into behavioral evidence, exposing APIs, strings, file paths, registry references, command aliases, metadata, and ATT&CK-mapped evidence traces that defenders can actually use. Practical local triage starts with recovering the proprietary format layer: once the analysis surface is visible, defenders can perform fast, explainable, and defensible detection without cloud submission.

sessions.title: Continuous Post-Exploitation Social Engineering: Don't Stop At Initial Access, Use It Until The End
sessions.abstract: Continuous Post-Exploitation Social Engineering: Don't Stop At Initial Access, Use It Until The End Yoann Dequeker | Red Team Leader, Wavestone Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Humans Factors, Enterprise Security Vault Recording: TBD Modern enterprise security strategies invest heavily in technical security stacks (MFA, EDR, and SOC) to hinder an attacker's stealthy progression. Yet, these systems remain operated and managed by humans who are fundamentally unpatchable. Is it possible to shift from software exploitation to "human exploitation" during a real-world attack? We move beyond the traditional view of Social Engineering (SE) as a mere initial access vector; we demonstrate its capabilities as a continuous weapon across all steps of the attack kill chain. Drawing from high-stakes Red Team "war stories" from 2025 to 2026 operations, we detail how the application of psychological principles can snowball minor technical vulnerabilities into full company compromise. We analyze the real world impact of social engineering as a tool for initial access, privilege escalation, lateral movement, access persistence, alert de-escalation, and evidence tampering. Step into a circus where technical exploits are sidelined in favor of psychological warfare between the red team, the blue team, and everyone caught in the middle. We will explore scenarios where security teams are forced to breach their own networks while attackers watch crisis response cells turn against themselves. You will leave with a compelling story, a redefined understanding of how attackers can leverage social engineering, and a blueprint for building architectural resilience that assumes human failure as a constant. Takeaway Social engineering is not limited to external phishing: Understand how social engineering can complement technical exploits throughout the entire attack lifecycle. See how it can be used to escalate privileges to Global Admin, de-escalate SOC alerts, and extend the lifespan of an operation by weeks following initial detection. The Helpdesk Vulnerability: Learn how the service-oriented KPIs of IT support (and equivalent teams) inadvertently create security breaches. Prioritizing ticket resolution speed over security compliance opens the door for attackers to gaslight IT staff. Architectural Resilience over Awareness: Gain a framework for transitioning from "Zero Human Error" targets toward post-compromise architectures. This approach focuses on SE-resistant technologies and restrictive conditional access policies rather than repetitive user training.

sessions.title: Crashing the Paper Airplane: How Telegram's 0-Click Parsers, E2EE Defaults, and Bug Bounty Program Fall Short
sessions.abstract: Crashing the Paper Airplane: How Telegram's 0-Click Parsers, E2EE Defaults, and Bug Bounty Program Fall Short Saifeldeen (wr3nchsr) Aziz | Security Researcher, Cyshield Ibrahim (the storm) ElSayed | Security Engineer Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 16:20-17:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Offense, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Telegram markets itself as a private messenger to more than one billion users. We put that claim under the light: which conversations are end-to-end encrypted? Can Telegram's servers observe what is being shared inside an encrypted chat? We answer these questions through a deep, cross-platform implementation review of Telegram's Android, iOS, and Desktop clients. We examine default Cloud Chats, which trust Telegram's servers, and Secret Chats, which must remain secure even when the server is malicious. One application provides the same messaging features under two opposing threat models while reusing shared resources, media pipelines, and native parsers. During the Briefing, we will discuss at least five vulnerability groups comprising two zero-click and three one-click attack paths. The findings include out-of-bounds reads and writes, type confusion, stack and heap corruption, and bypasses of Telegram's client-side fixes and observed server-side mitigations. Collectively, they affect Telegram's official Android, iOS and Desktop clients. Demos will include Secret Chat privacy failures and leaks, plenty of crashes, and remote code execution through a zero-click memory-corruption chain. The Briefing closes by examining Telegram's bug bounty program, which in my view is at odds with current industry practice. Based on our experience, its technical triage was weak, its rewards were below comparable programs, and the terms offered to us restricted publication. These factors discourage security research. The results are visible in the product: incomplete fixes, long patch gaps, and low-hanging attack surfaces that survive far longer than they should. You'll leave this Briefing with an evidence-based understanding of Telegram's actual privacy boundaries, a technical walkthrough of multiple zero-click paths from message delivery to code execution, and a practical way to assess how architecture, patching, and bounty incentives combine to shape security. Takeaway Telegram Users: Telegram's privacy messaging is broader than the protections its product actually provides. Attendees will learn to distinguish Cloud Chats from Secret Chats, identify which information can still cross the E2EE boundary, and determine whether Telegram's defaults and guarantees match their expectations. Security professionals: Attendees will receive a deep technical analysis of five vulnerability groups across Telegram's Android, iOS, and Desktop clients, including their reachability, root causes, exploit primitives, attempted fixes, and subsequent bypasses. They will see why server-side validation cannot replace root-cause client remediation and how these failures progress from privacy leaks to zero-click memory corruption and potential RCE. Telegram: Telegram should modernize its bug bounty program with technically competent triage, predictable terms that preserve researchers' ability to publish, and impact-driven rewards.

sessions.title: Dendrochronology Attacks: Breaking TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Without Breaking the TEE
sessions.abstract: Dendrochronology Attacks: Breaking TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Without Breaking the TEE Zachary Espiritu | Senior Research Engineer / Visiting Researcher, MongoDB Research / New York University Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cryptography, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD Arborists use dendrochronology, or the study of visible "growth rings" of a tree (as in, the plant), to infer past environmental events. We identify an analogous, exploitable phenomenon in the B+-tree indexes used by several encrypted databases (EDBs) based on trusted execution environments (TEEs). Many TEE-based EDBs have been shown to leak the order of indexed values, but not the histogram (or frequency of each value), with respect to a weaker class of snapshot adversaries who receive point-in-time snapshots of the database state. Because order-only leakage is strictly weaker than leaking both order and frequency, this order-only leakage substantially reduces the impact of possible plaintext inference attacks. We show that, in fact, you can recover frequency information from snapshots of a large set of TEE-based EDBs, even if the TEE itself is assumed to be "secure". Our insight is surprisingly simple: practical storage engines must impose a strict total order on indexed keys. They typically do so by augmenting each key with a public, totally ordered tie-breaker (e.g., record ID). While the tie-breakers are not necessarily sensitive, we show that, if the adversary learns information about the tie-breakers associated with each key, the adversary can recover the frequencies of plaintext keys. This, in turn, enables substantially stronger inference attacks. Our snapshot attacks apply to industry TEE-based encrypted databases including Microsoft SQL Server's Always Encrypted and Alibaba Cloud's Always-Confidential (as well as leading academic constructions). We will show experiments demonstrating how the addition of frequencies enables end-to-end inference attacks: for example, we show that extracting frequencies raises plaintext recovery from 0.1% to 97.6% on some datasets. At the end, we identify some broader lessons from this study on how end-to-end encrypted databases (and, more broadly, TEE-based applications that reuse existing components) should be developed and reviewed in practice. Takeaway Attendees will understand how plaintext implementation details in Microsoft SQL Server's Always Encrypted (and other databases) cause it to unintentionally leak histogram information to a weak snapshot adversary. Attendees will learn how this histogram information can leak a significant amount of information that allows an attacker to reconstruct significant information about the underlying plaintext data. This vulnerability wasn't found by anyone for a long time! This general research direction indicates there is probably other TEE-based applications that rely on existing plaintext algorithms that are silently hiding exploitable behavior. More broadly, TEE-based applications need very careful analysis, especially if they are relying on prior plaintext code.

sessions.title: Escape the Ether: Breaking Out of a VM Through a Network Accelerator Card
sessions.abstract: Escape the Ether: Breaking Out of a VM Through a Network Accelerator Card Thierry Fernandes Faria | Security Researcher, Intel Corporation Daniel Medina Velazquez | Security Researcher, Intel Corporation Igor Chervatyuk | Security Researcher, Intel Corporation Anders Fogh | Intel Fellow, Intel Corporation Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Platform Security, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Virtualized accelerator devices allow cloud tenants to achieve higher performance for their networking, graphics, and AI workloads. But they come with a significantly increased attack surface – offering new paths for a malicious guest to escape their VM and take over the host. In this Briefing, we will show how we abused a network card's SRIOV communication path to escape from a guest VM and directly obtain arbitrary code execution with host kernel privileges. All of this without having to worry about userland protections or hypervisor sandboxes, as this attack vector is independent of the specific hypervisor used. We will explore how the attack surface applies broadly across SRIOV HW accelerator drivers, making it especially relevant for IaaS public cloud deployments. We will walk through our guest-to-host kernel code execution exploit journey, including the techniques we used to heap spray the host's kernel from a guest VM and bypass mitigations like KASLR. Finally, we will share our solution for comprehensively fuzzing virtual IO interfaces to identify this class of vulnerability, and argue that device driver security must be treated not just as a traditional LPE surface, but also increasingly as a first-class VM escape boundary. Takeaway Learn how kernel exploitation looks different when the attacker is a guest VM rather than a user process — including why SMAP/SMEP become irrelevant, how to heap spray a host kernel from inside a VM, and how KASLR bypass changes in this context. Understand why virtual IO control planes in host kernel drivers can represent a VM escape boundary. This perspective is critical for threat modeling and driver assurance in virtualized environments. Learn how to leverage syzkaller's grammar-based fuzzing engine to effectively fuzz virtual IO interfaces in host kernel drivers.

sessions.title: Every Cloud Everywhere All at Once: Inside a Multi-Cloud Credentials & Data Theft Campaign
sessions.abstract: Every Cloud Everywhere All at Once: Inside a Multi-Cloud Credentials & Data Theft Campaign Sapir Federovsky | Security Engineer, Wiz (Google) Maayan Bentor | Security Engineer, Wiz (Google) Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Threat Hunting & Incident Response, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD What happens when an Azure specialist and a GCP expert compare notes on two seemingly isolated alerts? Initially, each of us thought they were observing another pen test, albeit a cloud-savvy one. However, after matching IOCs and spotting the same IP address striking two completely different organizations across two different cloud platforms at the same time, we realized we were looking at something much more interesting. This was a sophisticated, real-world threat actor operating across multiple cloud ecosystems simultaneously. This is the story of how we hunted this adversary from the very first anomaly to the heart-pounding moments we watched them move laterally through a production network in real-time, praying the client would wake up and see our high-severity alerts before it was too late. Most attackers specialize in one environment, but this campaign shattered the rulebook. We will break down how the attacker seamlessly jumped between Azure, GCP, AWS, and SaaS platforms (Okta, GitHub, and Snowflake), targeting dozens of organizations across unrelated sectors by enumerating environments, exfiltrating massive amounts of secrets, and executing highly selective data extraction. Takeaway A rare real-world documentation of a coordinated multi-cloud threat actor operating at an expert level - We present a unique investigation of a single adversary operating across Azure, GCP, AWS, and SaaS platforms, demonstrating consistent tooling, infrastructure reuse, and behavioral patterns across multiple unrelated organizations and cloud environments. Exposed long-lived cloud credentials remain one of the most dangerous attack paths in modern environments. When attached to highly privileged permissions, they become the Achilles' heel of every organization. Practical methods for detecting large-scale cloud campaigns using small, high-confidence behavioral signals. We demonstrate how seemingly low-signal indicators, such as API enumeration patterns, shared VPN infrastructure, and consistent user-agent strings, can be combined to reliably identify and track a coordinated, multi-cloud intrusion campaign with high confidence.

sessions.title: Eyes on the Edge: From an In-the-Wild AitM Framework to an IP-Camera Vulnerability Chain
sessions.abstract: Eyes on the Edge: From an In-the-Wild AitM Framework to an IP-Camera Vulnerability Chain NOT AVAILABLE ON-DEMAND Chi-en (Ashley) Shen | Security Research Engineering Technical Leader, Cisco Talos Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Threat Hunting & Incident Response, Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT Vault Recording: TBD IP-camera vulnerabilities are usually disclosed as isolated product bugs. This Briefing fills the gap that disclosures often leave: how familiar IoT failures become operational capability for a real attacker, and how that capability supports the attacker's broader operational objectives. Through attacker code, implant reverse engineering, packet evidence, root-cause analysis, and an end-to-end exploit demonstration, we connect the vulnerability chain to live, edge-resident AitM tradecraft. In February 2026, we disclosed DKnife, a Linux-based adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) framework deployed on edge devices to inspect and manipulate traffic for malware delivery, user activity monitoring, DNS hijacking, and binary-download hijacking on Windows and Android. While reversing DKnife, we found an undisclosed module built to obtain snapshots from IP cameras. Using that module as a roadmap, we reconstructed the workflow against an IP camera across firmware, mobile application, and cloud services. This investigation led to three vulnerabilities being disclosed under coordinated disclosure. Chained together, these flaws allow an attacker who can intercept camera-cloud traffic to force a fresh camera capture and recover the resulting upload without a camera account, cloud compromise, or breaking TLS cryptography. The impact extends beyond consumer privacy. IP cameras are increasingly relevant to nation-state operations, including reconnaissance, targeting support, and post-strike damage assessment. The EU Cyber Resilience Act reflects this shift by treating smart-home security products, including security cameras, as Class I "important products" subject to stronger lifecycle and conformity obligations. This case shows why that matters: without enforceable lifecycle accountability, devices deployed for safety can become distributed intelligence sensors for adversaries. We will walk through the full chain, from DKnife reverse engineering to camera firmware root-cause analysis and successful exploitation demonstration. We will also share practical guidance for users, vendors, and defenders, including DKnife indicators of compromise and detection logic for similar edge-resident AitM activity. Available in-person only, not recorded for on-demand viewing. Takeaway A real, in-the-wild surveillance framework ships a module built to steal IP-camera snapshots at the network edge. We reverse-engineered the camera to find out exactly how, and the answer is a chain of vulnerabilities anyone on-path can exploit with no credentials. For defenders / blue teams: concrete on-the-wire signatures and IOCs to detect both the camera attack and DKnife's camera module, and what a correct firmware/cloud fix looks like. Understand the impact of this vulnerability class under the upcoming Cyber Resilience Act requirements. For vulnerability researchers / IoT hackers: understanding the cloud-mediated IoT device analysis approach, and how the vulnerability details analysis can be facilitated by AI (AI helped to identify the firmware and RE). How hunting in the wild samples can reveal 0days. For leadership/policy makers: mass-market, cloud-connected cameras can be turned into on-demand sensors by capable, in-the-wild frameworks, and an optional, defeatable encryption "fix" offers false assurance. This strengthens the case for baseline security requirements for consumer IoT (no fail-open TLS, secure-by-default encryption, anti-replay) and enforceable coordinated-disclosure expectations.

sessions.title: From Wind Farm to CHP Plant: The Story of Lateral Movement in a Polish Energy Sector Attack
sessions.abstract: From Wind Farm to CHP Plant: The Story of Lateral Movement in a Polish Energy Sector Attack Marcin Dudek | Head of CERT.PL, CERT.PL Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT, Threat Hunting & Incident Response Vault Recording: TBD On December 29, 2025, Poland's energy sector was hit by what we believe was the first destructive cyber sabotage attack against energy infrastructure in NATO. Our initial report described attacks against 30 renewable energy sites and a large combined heat and power plant. But one piece of the incident was still missing - and it led to an attack path we had never seen in the wild before. This Briefing goes behind the scenes of the investigation into a second, smaller CHP plant affected during the same campaign. What first looked like human error turned into a three-month hunt through false leads, forgotten remote access devices, wiped industrial hardware, cellular connectivity, and infrastructure that was assumed to be isolated. The Briefing ends with lessons on private APN security, OT incident response, and handling large-scale cyber incidents involving critical infrastructure. Takeaway Treat private APNs as potential attack vectors, not trusted networks. Reconstruct multi-stage OT attack paths using hypothesis-driven validation. Recognize when hardware-level analysis is necessary and beneficial in OT incident response.

sessions.title: FrostyMorph & Friends: Reverse Engineering Secret Blizzard's .NET Arsenal
sessions.abstract: FrostyMorph & Friends: Reverse Engineering Secret Blizzard's .NET Arsenal AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Andreas Klopsch | Reverse Engineer, Microsoft Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Reverse Engineering, Malware Vault Recording: TBD This Briefing delivers an in-depth technical analysis of advanced .NET malware and associated tooling attributed to the nation-state APT group Secret Blizzard (Federal Security Service (FSB)). Our Briefing begins with ShadowWraith, a sophisticated and highly modular .NET backdoor engineered for long-term persistence and equipped with an extensive command-and-control (C2) channel. The analysis covers its architecture and execution flow, highlighting how individual modules can be dynamically loaded at runtime. We examine its configuration handling, command-and-control protocol and loadable modules. ShadowWraith stands out due to its emphasis on establishing a secure communication channel protected by multiple layers of encryption, including a flexible cryptographic design that can alter communication behavior based on configuration. Next, we examine FrostyStash, a multi-component framework consisting of an orchestrator, a system module, and a network module. FrostyStash is notable for its unique inter-component communication, achieved through abuse of the Windows Messaging subsystem to relay data across all three components. We dissect the communication model in detail, along with the role of each component within the framework. Additionally, we provide a timeline of changes introduced to FrostyStash by analyzing its evolution over time, highlighting key implementation differences and evolutionary trends. In the final part of the Briefing, we present a deep-dive analysis of FrostyMorph, a custom .NET obfuscator deployed alongside FrostyStash. FrostyMorph abuses .NET GUID streams to conceal string decryption keys within metadata, significantly increasing reverse-engineering complexity. In addition to analyzing its obfuscation strategy, we discuss how we approached this obfuscator and developed a custom deobfuscator to accelerate our analysis workflow. The deobfuscator will be released alongside this research and made available to the security community. We conclude with key takeaways, lessons learned throughout the investigation, and practical insights for defenders and malware analysts facing similar techniques in future campaigns. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Attendees will gain a deeper understanding of how modern espionage malware is structured. Through ShadowWraith and FrostyStash, we show two very different approaches to modular malware design, command-and-control frameworks, and long-term operational flexibility. Attendees will learn how .NET GUID streams can be abused to store runtime cryptographic material and complicate static analysis. We also demonstrate practical techniques for reversing and deobfuscating this protection mechanism that can be adapted for automated analysis workflows. Attendees will gain an understanding of how layered malware communication protocols are designed and implemented. By walking through ShadowWraith's command-and-control protocol, attendees will see how encryption, integrity checks, and configurable protocol layers work together to protect and obfuscate malware communications.

sessions.title: God Mode at the Border: Compromising Global Passport, Visa, and Immigration Systems
sessions.abstract: God Mode at the Border: Compromising Global Passport, Visa, and Immigration Systems Eaton Zveare | Independent Security Researcher Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Offense, Privacy Vault Recording: TBD Join me for a deep-dive into new vulnerabilities affecting international border control infrastructure. Full abstract coming soon. Takeaway Coming soon.

sessions.title: How AI Browser Extensions Hand Attackers the Keys to Your Browser
sessions.abstract: How AI Browser Extensions Hand Attackers the Keys to Your Browser Yichi Zhang | Security Researcher, Bytedance Yusong Guo | Security Expert, Bytedance Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Track : AI & ML: Attack and Defense Vault Recording: TBD AI browser extensions are rapidly evolving from chat sidebars to page manipulators and finally to agentic browser controllers, with their permission demands growing sharply. Our comparative analysis of manifests from 1,000+ extensions reveals that AI extensions request dangerous permissions such as "debugger" at significantly higher rates than traditional extensions. The combination of high-risk permissions and agentic capabilities creates a new and widely overlooked attack surface. Firstly, we propose a unified threat model for AI browser extensions, and identify multiple attack surfaces in their communication design — including unauthenticated message bridges, external Agent channels that can be hijacked, and injection-driven malicious tool calls. Our research uncovered multiple Critical-severity 0-day vulnerabilities affecting millions of users. By simply visiting a malicious webpage, a victim's extension can be hijacked to steal cross-origin data, take over the browser, or even execute arbitrary code. This is the first systematic security assessment of AI browser extensions from architecture to exploitation, delivering a reusable threat model and an open-source audit tool. Takeaway Master the unified threat model for AI browser extensions: understand the communication links of both Agent-in-Extension and WebBridge architectures, and the principles and exploitation methods of three attack surfaces — Unauthenticated Message Bridge, External Bridge Hijack, and Injection → Malicious Tool Call. Through 7 real-world 0-day cases, understand how these attack surfaces manifest in mainstream products, and why traditional origin validation and token authentication cannot cover all attack surfaces. Gain actionable audit methodologies and defense recommendations: use chrome-ext-audit and the source-to-sink analysis framework for systematic security assessment of AI browser extensions, along with targeted mitigation guidance for developers (communication channel authentication and tool call allowlisting), platforms (specialized AI extension security review), and end users (identifying excessive permissions and data exfiltration behavior).

sessions.title: IonStack: 1-Click Browser to Kernel Full-Chain to Get Root Shell on Android 17
sessions.abstract: IonStack: 1-Click Browser to Kernel Full-Chain to Get Root Shell on Android 17 Frank Wu | Co-founder, Nebula Security Xiaochuan Yu | Co-founder, Nebula Security Yuan Tan | Co-founder, Nebula Security Eten Zou | Co-founder, Nebula Security Juefei Pu | Master Student, University of California Riverside Alex Wu | Bachelor Student, UC San Diego Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD This Briefing presents IonStack, a 1-click chain that takes a stock Pixel 10 from a single web page to a root shell on Android 17, the first root on that release. We use two 0-days to demonstrate a full-chain browser-to-kernel exploit affecting Firefox versions before 151.0.3 and every Linux distribution of the last 15 years. The first 0-day is CVE-2026-10702, a miscompilation in Firefox's JavaScript JIT. In April 2026, Anthropic's Mythos helped harden Firefox with hundreds of vulnerability patches shipped right before Pwn2Own, which caused all 7 teams to withdraw their submissions and kept the target unclaimed. However, we found the one Mythos still missed and used it with a new browser exploit technique to get a stable remote code execution in the browser. The second is GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a 15-year-old (stack-)use-after-free in the Linux kernel's futex priority-inheritance path. Exploitable stack vulnerabilities are almost extinct in the modern kernel. And we turned GhostLock from a single constrained kernel write to full root under KASLR and KCFI. We will discuss the root causes of the two 0-days and how we chained them together to get a reliable, one-click root of Android 17. An online demo is available at https://rootme.nebusec.io Takeaway How a browser JIT flaw and GhostLock chain from a single web page to root on Android 17, and where each mitigation layer holds and where it does not. How to turn an extremely constrained leakless write primitive on the newest Android kernel to get root and escape seccomp in practice, from a KASLR leak to KCFI bypass, and eventually to full kernel read and write. A new technique for turning a Firefox JIT bug into stable, reusable code execution with WASM trick.

sessions.title: Keys Under the Doormat: From MQTT to Mass Vehicle Compromise
sessions.abstract: Keys Under the Doormat: From MQTT to Mass Vehicle Compromise AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Linfeng Xiao | Senior Security Researcher, Ying'ao Chen | Director of Product Security, Unitree Robotics Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Hardware / Embedded, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD TLS, mutual authentication, and ACLs are widely treated as the security baseline for MQTT in connected vehicles. Our research shows that this assumption is incomplete. Across real production deployments, we found a repeatable failure mode in which attackers who gain or mint valid identities can still break tenant boundaries, poison authorization logic, and pivot from embedded messaging channels into cloud and vehicle-adjacent functions. We call this pattern Post-Auth Collapse (PAC). This Briefing turns PAC into a practical offensive and defensive model. We show how credentials can be recovered from apps, firmware, and cloud issuance flows; how topic namespace and wildcard semantics can undermine broker authorization; and how a single authenticated foothold can scale into cross-tenant or cross-brand impact. The talk is grounded in sanitized case studies spanning 11 major OEMs and 18 production models, representing more than 5 million potentially affected vehicles. Attendees will leave with a root-cause taxonomy, reproducible validation methodology, and a concrete hardening checklist for MQTT-based embedded platforms. The goal is to help defenders move beyond "baseline controls deployed" and toward authorization designs that still hold under real adversarial conditions. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Why the automotive industry's "MQTT is fixed" narrative is dangerously incomplete: PAC shows how attackers can turn a single valid session into cross-tenant, cross-brand, and fleet-scale impact. How to reproduce PAC in the real world using repeatable techniques for credential acquisition, privileged identity abuse, namespace manipulation, and cross-protocol pivoting. How to actually defend connected-vehicle MQTT systems when mTLS, ACLs, and hardened credential storage are not enough on their own.

sessions.title: Kinetic Prompt Injection: Agent Compromise With a Physical Blast Radius
sessions.abstract: Kinetic Prompt Injection: Agent Compromise With a Physical Blast Radius Pliny the Liberator | Steward & Strike Lead, BT6 Adrian (threlfall) Wood | Frontier AI Red Team Operator, BT6 Sean (seahop) Hopkins | Frontier AI Red Team Operator, BT6 Eito "eimi80" Miyamura | Frontier AI Red Team Operator, BT6 Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Hardware / Embedded Vault Recording: TBD Prompt injection is usually treated as a text problem contained on a screen: a bad output, leaked data, a rogue tool call. Here, the compromised agent controls a robot. We demonstrate a live jailbreak of a Unitree Go2 robot dog connected to Gemini Robotics, reached through its own camera and microphone and driven to physical movement without a human approving each action. The robot acts on the attacker's instructions. For Black Hat Europe, we extend our US briefing with simulated sleeper-agent demonstrations: normal behavior until a trigger activates malicious behavior. We connect these results to our previous robot-to-robot worm research, examining immediate compromise, delayed activation, and propagation. Underneath the demos is a measurement problem. A clean evaluation does not establish that unsafe behavior is gone. Test conditions can leave triggers untested, and evaluation cues can change how an agent behaves. We trace the failures from sensory input through model decisions to physical action, distinguish model-level attacks from platform compromise, and show what defenders need to test: whose instructions the agent follows, when its behavior changes, and whether controls can stop an unauthorized action even when the model permits it. Live hardware on stage, with extended scenarios in simulation. Takeaway Coming Soon.

sessions.title: Living Off the Agent: Exploiting the Root Daemon Every Cloud VM Trusts
sessions.abstract: Living Off the Agent: Exploiting the Root Daemon Every Cloud VM Trusts Shaul Ben Hai | Security Researcher, SentinelOne Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Track : Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD Every EC2 instance and GCP VM runs a management agent as root. These agents — AWS Systems Manager and GCP Guest/OSConfig — receive commands from the cloud control plane and execute them with full system privileges. Despite running on hundreds of millions of VMs, their internals have never been comprehensively audited. We changed that. We performed the first source-level offensive audit of both agents, reverse-engineering their plugin execution models, IPC mechanisms, update paths, and offline execution modes. We discovered that both clouds independently ship the same design-level flaw: a single coarse IAM permission grants unaudited root code execution through a trusted daemon, with no payload signature and no execution-specific audit event. On AWS, we present a class of five vulnerabilities in the SSM agent's plugin model — not isolated bugs, but a design flaw. We demonstrate restricted "download-only" IAM principals achieving arbitrary root writes, environment variable injection enabling root code execution with zero malicious command body, and unsigned artifact fetch running attacker code as both root and SYSTEM. We chain these into a complete kill chain: restricted-IAM to CloudTrail-blind root, self-healing persistence, fleet-wide silent compromise with forged compliance telemetry, and phantom instance injection — all proven live across Linux and Windows. On GCP, we reproduce the thesis through a novel, unpublished path: metadata-driven OSConfig recipe execution achieving root with no API call, no reboot, and no audit trail. We then show how every existing detection approach fails — ancestry rules defeated by daemonization, cloud correlation broken by audit-blind execution, host EDR blind to serverless SSM Automation — and present the detection framework that works by fusing host and cloud telemetry and alerting on their disagreements. Attendees will receive the full cross-cloud attack surface map, proof-of-concept demonstrations for every finding, and a working detection ruleset. Takeaway Deploy a detection ruleset that covers the complete cloud agent attack surface — including the paths your current EDR and CloudTrail monitoring miss entirely. Attendees receive a working, open-source detection framework that fuses host-level telemetry (process ancestry, file writes, network connections) with cloud-level API events, and alerts on disagreements between them — the signature of audit-blind agent execution. The ruleset covers Run Command, Session Manager, port-forwarding, offline execution, and daemonization-based evasion, closing gaps that process-ancestry-only or CloudTrail-only approaches leave wide open. Test the assumption that scoping IAM permissions to specific SSM document types (or GCP metadata operations) creates a meaningful security boundary. We prove across two clouds that "download-only," "update-only," and "metadata-only" IAM restrictions do not prevent root code execution — the agents execute every plugin as root with no sandboxing, no payload signature, and no path containment. Attendees can audit their own IAM policies for these illusory boundaries and replace them with controls that actually hold: instance-level network segmentation, mandatory document approval workflows, and host-side execution monitoring. Identify and remediate a new class of persistence and anti-forensics techniques that live in the cloud control plane, not on the instance disk — surviving reimaging, evading forensic acquisition, and auto-enrolling new infrastructure. We demonstrate State Manager tag-targeted associations (payload in the cloud, not on disk, auto-captures new instances), CloudTrail-blind local execution directories, and forged inventory that reports false compliance

sessions.title: Lost in Translation: The Systemic Auth Flaws Hiding in Every Identity Broker
sessions.abstract: Lost in Translation: The Systemic Auth Flaws Hiding in Every Identity Broker Zixu Zhou | PhD Student, University of Toronto David Lie | Professor, University of Toronto Xiangyu Guo | PhD Student, University of Toronto Ilya Grishchenko | Postdoc, University of Toronto Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Enterprise Security, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD Keycloak. Dex. Authentik. Zitadel. Logto. Casdoor. If your company does single sign-on, one of these identity brokers sits in the middle of everything, taking a login from your identity provider and turning it into a session for every app and cloud service behind it. It's a man-in-the-middle you installed on purpose. And when it gets authentication wrong, none of those downstream apps can even tell: by the time they see a session, the broker has already vouched for it. So we asked one question: what does a broker have to get right that a normal app doesn't? The answer is that a broker wears two hats at once: it's a client of the IdP above it and an IdP to the apps below it. Every auth spec, and almost every line of broker code, is written as if each party wears only one. That one wrong assumption is a vulnerability factory. To prove it, we built PORTA: it turns five broker-specific security rules into concrete attack sequences, fires them at live brokers, and decides mechanically whether each one worked. It found 33 previously unknown vulnerabilities across all seven brokers — written by different teams, in four languages — and the same handful of flaws keeps reappearing: MFA skipped entirely if you come in through SSO, an attacker's own IdP accepted as the trusted one, a token minted for one service accepted by every other, and full account takeover through unverified email linking. We'll show these live, explain why independent teams keep writing the identical bug, and hand you the exact request-level checks to run against your own broker before someone else does. Everything was responsibly disclosed — the work has already produced 19 CVEs, ten of them rated Critical (CVSS 9.0+). Takeaway A threat model you can act on: why identity brokers are riskier than the apps behind them, and five concrete "trust-translation" rules you can use to audit any broker — vendor or home-grown — the day you get back. Four attacks you can reproduce, with the exact request-level tell for each: MFA bypass, trust-anchor bypass, cross-service token replay, and account takeover — against brokers you probably run. A tool that does it for you: we open-source PORTA so you can point it at your own broker and find these before an attacker does.

sessions.title: MCPocalypse: When the Universal Connector Meets Reality
sessions.abstract: MCPocalypse: When the Universal Connector Meets Reality Yotam Perkal | Director, Security Research, Pluto Security Gil Maman | Co founder & CTO, Pluto Security Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 16:20-17:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Enterprise Security Vault Recording: TBD The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is becoming the default way AI agents connect to cloud accounts, source control, and internal APIs. In just two years, it has evolved from a specification into production infrastructure, deployed on developer laptops and inside corporate VPCs, holding real credentials and performing real work on behalf of users who never considered it a network service. Over the last year, we conducted what we believe is the largest systematic security audit of the MCP ecosystem to date. We have identified and reported over 100 vulnerabilities across popular open-source and vendor-official MCP servers, 53 are already public, 39 have assigned CVEs, and more than 50 remain in ongoing coordinated disclosure or follow-up. The affected projects represent a who's who of the ecosystem: Microsoft, Google, AWS, Dropbox, Hugging Face, Cloudflare, Docker, IBM, ByteDance, CircleCI, GitLab, Neo4j, Anthropic-adjacent projects, and dozens more, often spanning multiple MCP servers from the same vendor. Three attack surfaces recur throughout the ecosystem: •Server implementation vulnerabilities: SSRF through unvalidated URL headers and credential forwarding, arbitrary file writes leading to remote code execution, unauthenticated management endpoints, and sandbox escapes. •DNS rebinding of local MCP servers: Any webpage a developer opens can potentially reach their agent's tools and act with the developer's credentials. This was our largest single finding class, affecting more than 50 servers. •Model-layer abuse: MCP servers can become conduits for indirect prompt injection or targets for tool squatting, turning trust between agents, tools, and users into an attack surface. We will explain our audit methodology, demonstrate three live exploit chains, one for each attack surface, and present the ecosystem-wide patterns that emerge from our research and findings from the broader security community. We will also share the AI-driven security-evaluation process that made an audit of this scale possible and release mcp_binder, our open-source DNS-rebinding lab for MCP servers, which we will also present at Black Hat Europe Arsenal. Takeaway An evidence-based, ecosystem-wide picture of the MCP attack surface. Attendees will leave with a three-surface threat model (implementation / DNS rebinding / model), the recurring failure patterns in each, and the ability to reason about MCP risk in their own environment. Reproducible tooling to test their own deployments. mcp_binder for DNS-rebinding assessment of local MCP servers, the first public tool we know of for this specific attack class against MCPs, and an MCP Security Evaluation Skill for source-review-driven audits at scale. Both aimed to be released open-source in conjunction with the briefing (we also submitted mcp_binder to the Arsenal CFP). Three role-specific hardening checklists and tips (for MCP builders, deployers/users, and security researchers), each distilled from the failure modes we saw repeat across the vulnerability pool.

sessions.title: MIDImorphosis - Exploiting a Windows 11 Privilege Escalation Vulnerability with a Teensy USB Device
sessions.abstract: MIDImorphosis - Exploiting a Windows 11 Privilege Escalation Vulnerability with a Teensy USB Device Andy Davis | Global Research Director, NCC Group Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Windows 11 shipped an entirely new kernel driver stack that almost nobody has looked at yet: Windows MIDI Services, Microsoft's ground-up, partially open-source rewrite of USB MIDI support. We found a kernel memory corruption bug in it, reachable the instant a device is plugged in and spent the following months turning it into something far more dangerous than a crash: a local SYSTEM shell exploit. This Briefing tells that story end to end. We'll show how the bug was found, how we proved that it's a genuine code-execution primitive and not just a fuzzer curiosity and then walk through what it actually took to weaponise it. Modern Windows makes every step of that journey hard : reliable heap grooming on the segment heap, defeating kASLR, stealing and forging a privileged token, bypassing an impersonation check, dodging a kernel corruption defense that's specifically designed to stop exactly this kind of attack. We solved all of it, and we'll show you how the pieces fit together, including a few tricks we haven't seen described anywhere else. Then we go physical. We collapsed the entire chain (payload delivery and kernel exploitation) onto a single USB implant built from cheap off-the-shelf hardware. It looks like an ordinary USB stick, delivers itself and quietly morphs into the weaponised device once its work is done. No operator laptop, no network connection back to the attacker, nothing to notice. We'll plug it into a Windows 11 machine on stage and let you watch what happens. If you work on Windows kernel security, USB vulnerability research, or physical red-teaming, you'll leave with techniques you can use and a different sense of what "don't plug in a USB stick you don't trust" actually has to defend against. Takeaway New doesn't mean safe and here's how to check. Freshly-shipped, actively-developed in-box Windows kernel drivers deserve the same adversarial scrutiny as legacy ones. Attendees leave with a concrete, repeatable methodology (adversarial USB descriptor emulation plus source-assisted decompilation) they can point at the next new class driver Microsoft ships and a specific code pattern (two-pass size-then-fetch descriptor parsing) worth grepping for. A reusable playbook for exploitation on modern Windows. Attendees get field-tested solutions to the failure modes that make kernel pool-overflow exploitation unreliable on segment-heap/LFH targets, grooming races, safe-unlink corruption, token forgery, kASLR defeat without a leak, that they can carry directly into their own exploit-dev work, on this bug or an entirely different one. Physical access is a bigger blast radius than most threat models assume. A live demonstration that an entire kernel 0-day chain, delivery and exploitation, collapses onto a single cheap implant with no operator infrastructure gives defenders a concrete, current benchmark for what can be achieved with a USB exploit in 2026.

sessions.title: No More Trampolines: The Missing Insert Primitive for Native Binary Editing
sessions.abstract: No More Trampolines: The Missing Insert Primitive for Native Binary Editing Ziyi Shen | Security Engineering Analyst, The World Bank Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Reverse Engineering Vault Recording: TBD Native binary editing is missing one of its basic atomic primitives: local insertion. Modern reverse engineering tools make it easy to overwrite existing instructions, but inserting bytes inside an already compiled executable while preserving its semantics remains unsupported in practice. Insertion is not just a larger patch. Replacement preserves layout; insertion changes it. Once bytes are inserted inside .text, nearby code moves while the binary's embedded assumptions about addresses and metadata remain tied to the old layout. Relative control-flow displacements, RIP-relative references, relocation-backed pointers, exception metadata, jump tables, security metadata, and compiler-generated structures may all need to stay synchronized. Missing even one hidden reference can cause silent corruption, delayed crashes, or broken control flow. This Briefing presents BinaryScalpel, a technique and tool for true in-place byte insertion in x64 PE binaries. Its core contribution is Segmented Absorption, an algorithm that uses compiler-generated alignment padding to absorb insertion shifts across multiple local regions instead of shifting the entire remaining .text section. This turns insertion from a broad relayout problem into a localized repair problem. The Briefing also develops a practical taxonomy of address-dependent structures found in real MSVC-compiled PE binaries, including DISP32_TEXT_PTR, inline jump tables, delay-import overlap, Control Flow Guard metadata, unwind handler RVAs, and relocation-backed absolute references. We evaluate BinaryScalpel across 78 real-world executables, including Windows utilities, Sysinternals tools, game binaries, and security software. The broader impact is two-sided: for reverse engineers, red teams, and instrumentation developers, local insertion enables modifications that previously required trampolines, code caves, or new sections; for defenders and malware analysts, it challenges PE tampering assumptions built around those structural artifacts. The takeaway is that in-place insertion is not merely another patching trick, but a missing primitive with practical consequences for both binary modification and detection. Takeaway A new mental model for native binary editing - Attendees will understand why local insertion is the missing atomic primitive in practical binary editing. Replacement preserves layout; insertion changes it. This distinction explains why a seemingly small edit can trigger a broad semantic repair problem across code, data, metadata, and compiler-generated structures.
