We trace the failures from sensory input through model decisions to physical action, distinguish model-level attacks from platform compromise, and show what defenders need to test: whose instructions the agent follows, when its behavior changes, and whether controls can stop an unauthorized action even when the model permits it. Live hardware on stage, with extended scenarios in simulation. Takeaway Coming Soon.

sessions.title: Living Off the Agent: Exploiting the Root Daemon Every Cloud VM Trusts
sessions.abstract: Living Off the Agent: Exploiting the Root Daemon Every Cloud VM Trusts Shaul Ben Hai | Security Researcher, SentinelOne Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Track : Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD Every EC2 instance and GCP VM runs a management agent as root. These agents — AWS Systems Manager and GCP Guest/OSConfig — receive commands from the cloud control plane and execute them with full system privileges. Despite running on hundreds of millions of VMs, their internals have never been comprehensively audited. We changed that. We performed the first source-level offensive audit of both agents, reverse-engineering their plugin execution models, IPC mechanisms, update paths, and offline execution modes. We discovered that both clouds independently ship the same design-level flaw: a single coarse IAM permission grants unaudited root code execution through a trusted daemon, with no payload signature and no execution-specific audit event. On AWS, we present a class of five vulnerabilities in the SSM agent's plugin model — not isolated bugs, but a design flaw. We demonstrate restricted "download-only" IAM principals achieving arbitrary root writes, environment variable injection enabling root code execution with zero malicious command body, and unsigned artifact fetch running attacker code as both root and SYSTEM. We chain these into a complete kill chain: restricted-IAM to CloudTrail-blind root, self-healing persistence, fleet-wide silent compromise with forged compliance telemetry, and phantom instance injection — all proven live across Linux and Windows. On GCP, we reproduce the thesis through a novel, unpublished path: metadata-driven OSConfig recipe execution achieving root with no API call, no reboot, and no audit trail. We then show how every existing detection approach fails — ancestry rules defeated by daemonization, cloud correlation broken by audit-blind execution, host EDR blind to serverless SSM Automation — and present the detection framework that works by fusing host and cloud telemetry and alerting on their disagreements. Attendees will receive the full cross-cloud attack surface map, proof-of-concept demonstrations for every finding, and a working detection ruleset. Takeaway Deploy a detection ruleset that covers the complete cloud agent attack surface — including the paths your current EDR and CloudTrail monitoring miss entirely. Attendees receive a working, open-source detection framework that fuses host-level telemetry (process ancestry, file writes, network connections) with cloud-level API events, and alerts on disagreements between them — the signature of audit-blind agent execution. The ruleset covers Run Command, Session Manager, port-forwarding, offline execution, and daemonization-based evasion, closing gaps that process-ancestry-only or CloudTrail-only approaches leave wide open. Test the assumption that scoping IAM permissions to specific SSM document types (or GCP metadata operations) creates a meaningful security boundary. We prove across two clouds that "download-only," "update-only," and "metadata-only" IAM restrictions do not prevent root code execution — the agents execute every plugin as root with no sandboxing, no payload signature, and no path containment. Attendees can audit their own IAM policies for these illusory boundaries and replace them with controls that actually hold: instance-level network segmentation, mandatory document approval workflows, and host-side execution monitoring. Identify and remediate a new class of persistence and anti-forensics techniques that live in the cloud control plane, not on the instance disk — surviving reimaging, evading forensic acquisition, and auto-enrolling new infrastructure. We demonstrate State Manager tag-targeted associations (payload in the cloud, not on disk, auto-captures new instances), CloudTrail-blind local execution directories, and forged inventory that reports false compliance

sessions.title: Lost in Translation: The Systemic Auth Flaws Hiding in Every Identity Broker
sessions.abstract: Lost in Translation: The Systemic Auth Flaws Hiding in Every Identity Broker Zixu Zhou | PhD Student, University of Toronto David Lie | Professor, University of Toronto Xiangyu Guo | PhD Student, University of Toronto Ilya Grishchenko | Postdoc, University of Toronto Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Enterprise Security, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD Keycloak. Dex. Authentik. Zitadel. Logto. Casdoor. If your company does single sign-on, one of these identity brokers sits in the middle of everything, taking a login from your identity provider and turning it into a session for every app and cloud service behind it. It's a man-in-the-middle you installed on purpose. And when it gets authentication wrong, none of those downstream apps can even tell: by the time they see a session, the broker has already vouched for it. So we asked one question: what does a broker have to get right that a normal app doesn't? The answer is that a broker wears two hats at once: it's a client of the IdP above it and an IdP to the apps below it. Every auth spec, and almost every line of broker code, is written as if each party wears only one. That one wrong assumption is a vulnerability factory. To prove it, we built PORTA: it turns five broker-specific security rules into concrete attack sequences, fires them at live brokers, and decides mechanically whether each one worked. It found 33 previously unknown vulnerabilities across all seven brokers — written by different teams, in four languages — and the same handful of flaws keeps reappearing: MFA skipped entirely if you come in through SSO, an attacker's own IdP accepted as the trusted one, a token minted for one service accepted by every other, and full account takeover through unverified email linking. We'll show these live, explain why independent teams keep writing the identical bug, and hand you the exact request-level checks to run against your own broker before someone else does. Everything was responsibly disclosed — the work has already produced 19 CVEs, ten of them rated Critical (CVSS 9.0+). Takeaway A threat model you can act on: why identity brokers are riskier than the apps behind them, and five concrete "trust-translation" rules you can use to audit any broker — vendor or home-grown — the day you get back. Four attacks you can reproduce, with the exact request-level tell for each: MFA bypass, trust-anchor bypass, cross-service token replay, and account takeover — against brokers you probably run. A tool that does it for you: we open-source PORTA so you can point it at your own broker and find these before an attacker does.

sessions.title: MCPocalypse: When the Universal Connector Meets Reality
sessions.abstract: MCPocalypse: When the Universal Connector Meets Reality Yotam Perkal | Director, Security Research, Pluto Security Gil Maman | Co founder & CTO, Pluto Security Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 16:20-17:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Enterprise Security Vault Recording: TBD The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is becoming the default way AI agents connect to cloud accounts, source control, and internal APIs. In just two years, it has evolved from a specification into production infrastructure, deployed on developer laptops and inside corporate VPCs, holding real credentials and performing real work on behalf of users who never considered it a network service. Over the last year, we conducted what we believe is the largest systematic security audit of the MCP ecosystem to date. We have identified and reported over 100 vulnerabilities across popular open-source and vendor-official MCP servers, 53 are already public, 39 have assigned CVEs, and more than 50 remain in ongoing coordinated disclosure or follow-up. The affected projects represent a who's who of the ecosystem: Microsoft, Google, AWS, Dropbox, Hugging Face, Cloudflare, Docker, IBM, ByteDance, CircleCI, GitLab, Neo4j, Anthropic-adjacent projects, and dozens more, often spanning multiple MCP servers from the same vendor. Three attack surfaces recur throughout the ecosystem: •Server implementation vulnerabilities: SSRF through unvalidated URL headers and credential forwarding, arbitrary file writes leading to remote code execution, unauthenticated management endpoints, and sandbox escapes. •DNS rebinding of local MCP servers: Any webpage a developer opens can potentially reach their agent's tools and act with the developer's credentials. This was our largest single finding class, affecting more than 50 servers. •Model-layer abuse: MCP servers can become conduits for indirect prompt injection or targets for tool squatting, turning trust between agents, tools, and users into an attack surface. We will explain our audit methodology, demonstrate three live exploit chains, one for each attack surface, and present the ecosystem-wide patterns that emerge from our research and findings from the broader security community. We will also share the AI-driven security-evaluation process that made an audit of this scale possible and release mcp_binder, our open-source DNS-rebinding lab for MCP servers, which we will also present at Black Hat Europe Arsenal. Takeaway An evidence-based, ecosystem-wide picture of the MCP attack surface. Attendees will leave with a three-surface threat model (implementation / DNS rebinding / model), the recurring failure patterns in each, and the ability to reason about MCP risk in their own environment. Reproducible tooling to test their own deployments. mcp_binder for DNS-rebinding assessment of local MCP servers, the first public tool we know of for this specific attack class against MCPs, and an MCP Security Evaluation Skill for source-review-driven audits at scale. Both aimed to be released open-source in conjunction with the briefing (we also submitted mcp_binder to the Arsenal CFP). Three role-specific hardening checklists and tips (for MCP builders, deployers/users, and security researchers), each distilled from the failure modes we saw repeat across the vulnerability pool.

sessions.title: MIDImorphosis - Exploiting a Windows 11 Privilege Escalation Vulnerability with a Teensy USB Device
sessions.abstract: MIDImorphosis - Exploiting a Windows 11 Privilege Escalation Vulnerability with a Teensy USB Device Andy Davis | Global Research Director, NCC Group Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD Windows 11 shipped an entirely new kernel driver stack that almost nobody has looked at yet: Windows MIDI Services, Microsoft's ground-up, partially open-source rewrite of USB MIDI support. We found a kernel memory corruption bug in it, reachable the instant a device is plugged in and spent the following months turning it into something far more dangerous than a crash: a local SYSTEM shell exploit. This Briefing tells that story end to end. We'll show how the bug was found, how we proved that it's a genuine code-execution primitive and not just a fuzzer curiosity and then walk through what it actually took to weaponise it. Modern Windows makes every step of that journey hard : reliable heap grooming on the segment heap, defeating kASLR, stealing and forging a privileged token, bypassing an impersonation check, dodging a kernel corruption defense that's specifically designed to stop exactly this kind of attack. We solved all of it, and we'll show you how the pieces fit together, including a few tricks we haven't seen described anywhere else. Then we go physical. We collapsed the entire chain (payload delivery and kernel exploitation) onto a single USB implant built from cheap off-the-shelf hardware. It looks like an ordinary USB stick, delivers itself and quietly morphs into the weaponised device once its work is done. No operator laptop, no network connection back to the attacker, nothing to notice. We'll plug it into a Windows 11 machine on stage and let you watch what happens. If you work on Windows kernel security, USB vulnerability research, or physical red-teaming, you'll leave with techniques you can use and a different sense of what "don't plug in a USB stick you don't trust" actually has to defend against. Takeaway New doesn't mean safe and here's how to check. Freshly-shipped, actively-developed in-box Windows kernel drivers deserve the same adversarial scrutiny as legacy ones. Attendees leave with a concrete, repeatable methodology (adversarial USB descriptor emulation plus source-assisted decompilation) they can point at the next new class driver Microsoft ships and a specific code pattern (two-pass size-then-fetch descriptor parsing) worth grepping for. A reusable playbook for exploitation on modern Windows. Attendees get field-tested solutions to the failure modes that make kernel pool-overflow exploitation unreliable on segment-heap/LFH targets, grooming races, safe-unlink corruption, token forgery, kASLR defeat without a leak, that they can carry directly into their own exploit-dev work, on this bug or an entirely different one. Physical access is a bigger blast radius than most threat models assume. A live demonstration that an entire kernel 0-day chain, delivery and exploitation, collapses onto a single cheap implant with no operator infrastructure gives defenders a concrete, current benchmark for what can be achieved with a USB exploit in 2026.

sessions.title: No More Trampolines: The Missing Insert Primitive for Native Binary Editing
sessions.abstract: No More Trampolines: The Missing Insert Primitive for Native Binary Editing Ziyi Shen | Security Engineering Analyst, The World Bank Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Reverse Engineering Vault Recording: TBD Native binary editing is missing one of its basic atomic primitives: local insertion. Modern reverse engineering tools make it easy to overwrite existing instructions, but inserting bytes inside an already compiled executable while preserving its semantics remains unsupported in practice. Insertion is not just a larger patch. Replacement preserves layout; insertion changes it. Once bytes are inserted inside .text, nearby code moves while the binary's embedded assumptions about addresses and metadata remain tied to the old layout. Relative control-flow displacements, RIP-relative references, relocation-backed pointers, exception metadata, jump tables, security metadata, and compiler-generated structures may all need to stay synchronized. Missing even one hidden reference can cause silent corruption, delayed crashes, or broken control flow. This Briefing presents BinaryScalpel, a technique and tool for true in-place byte insertion in x64 PE binaries. Its core contribution is Segmented Absorption, an algorithm that uses compiler-generated alignment padding to absorb insertion shifts across multiple local regions instead of shifting the entire remaining .text section. This turns insertion from a broad relayout problem into a localized repair problem. The Briefing also develops a practical taxonomy of address-dependent structures found in real MSVC-compiled PE binaries, including DISP32_TEXT_PTR, inline jump tables, delay-import overlap, Control Flow Guard metadata, unwind handler RVAs, and relocation-backed absolute references. We evaluate BinaryScalpel across 78 real-world executables, including Windows utilities, Sysinternals tools, game binaries, and security software. The broader impact is two-sided: for reverse engineers, red teams, and instrumentation developers, local insertion enables modifications that previously required trampolines, code caves, or new sections; for defenders and malware analysts, it challenges PE tampering assumptions built around those structural artifacts. The takeaway is that in-place insertion is not merely another patching trick, but a missing primitive with practical consequences for both binary modification and detection. Takeaway A new mental model for native binary editing - Attendees will understand why local insertion is the missing atomic primitive in practical binary editing. Replacement preserves layout; insertion changes it. This distinction explains why a seemingly small edit can trigger a broad semantic repair problem across code, data, metadata, and compiler-generated structures. A practical understanding of Segmented Absorption - Participants will learn how compiler-generated padding can be used to absorb insertion shifts across multiple local regions, transforming a naive whole-section shift into a bounded, zone-based repair problem. This model makes true in-place insertion practical without relying on trampolines, code caves, or new sections. The ability to reason about hidden layout dependencies and their security impact - The talk will show how real x64 PE binaries encode address assumptions far beyond relocation tables and visible instructions, including DISP32_TEXT_PTR, inline jump tables, CFG metadata, unwind handlers, delay-import overlap, relocation-backed pointers, and function-pointer RVAs. Attendees will also learn why these hidden dependencies matter for both binary modification and detection: they determine when patching techniques become fragile, and why PE tampering assumptions based on structural artifacts can weaken when local insertion becomes feasible.

sessions.title: ON-DEMAND - Breaking Linux Boot Trust: A UEFI Bootkit Across Shim, GRUB, and the Kernel
sessions.abstract: ON-DEMAND - Breaking Linux Boot Trust: A UEFI Bootkit Across Shim, GRUB, and the Kernel AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Alejandro Vázquez Vázquez | Vulnerability Researcher Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Malware, Reverse Engineering Vault Recording: TBD The Linux boot chain is built on a layered trust model where each component - from UEFI firmware through Shim, GRUB, and the kernel - verifies the next before passing control. Secure Boot, measured boot, and signature enforcement are designed to ensure that only authorized code executes before the operating system starts. However, the security of this model depends entirely on the integrity of every stage, and weaknesses at any point can subvert the entire trust foundation. While UEFI bootkits targeting Windows have been publicly documented and studied for years, the Linux boot chain has received significantly less attention from an offensive research perspective. Despite recent indicators that firmware-level threats against Linux are emerging, there is still no complete, publicly available UEFI bootkit implementation that can be studied and reproduced end to end. This Briefing presents a fully functional UEFI bootkit for Linux capable of hooking and modifying every stage of the boot chain in memory, from Shim through GRUB to the compressed kernel, enabling unsigned kernel code to execute on fully updated systems with Secure Boot enabled. We walk through the complete infection chain, demonstrating how each trust boundary is identified, targeted, and subverted through specific hooking and patching techniques at the firmware level. The Briefing covers the reverse engineering process required to understand the internal structures of each boot component, the specific techniques used to intercept and modify execution flow at each stage, how kernel integrity mechanisms are bypassed before the operating system initializes, and how the bootkit enables the deployment of kernel-level rootkits for post-compromise persistence. All source code, reverse engineering notes, and multiple Linux kernel rootkits will be publicly released, providing the security community with a complete framework to study, reproduce, and defend against firmware-level threats targeting Linux. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Understand how the Linux UEFI boot chain works internally, including the trust relationships between Shim, GRUB, and the kernel, and where the security-critical boundaries exist that can be targeted at the firmware level. Learn the specific reverse engineering and hooking techniques required to intercept and modify each stage of the Linux boot chain from UEFI, including how Secure Boot verification, kernel signature enforcement, and integrity mechanisms can be subverted in memory before the operating system initializes. Gain access to a complete, publicly released bootkit framework with full source code, kernel rootkits, and documentation, enabling security teams to reproduce firmware-level attacks against Linux systems for threat emulation, red team operations, and the development of detection and monitoring capabilities.

sessions.title: On-DEMAND - Glucose in the Air: Wireless Medical IoT Without a Trust Anchor
sessions.abstract: On-DEMAND - Glucose in the Air: Wireless Medical IoT Without a Trust Anchor AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Barłomiej Gorkiewicz | Senior Application Security Engineer, Doyensec LLC Mohamed Ouad | Senior Application Security Engineer, Doyensec LLC Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT, Hardware / Embedded Vault Recording: TBD Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) stream health information over Bluetooth Low Energy from body-worn sensors to smartphones and the vendors' clouds. Millions of people depend on this communication system every day. However, existing CGM regulations tend to focus on medical-device compliance and operational requirements, while their security posture as connected medical IoT devices is often not fully evaluated. Over a two-month period, we conducted a comparative security assessment of four commercial continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) sensors, covering wireless pairing mechanisms, mobile applications, embedded interfaces, and portions of the supporting cloud infrastructure. Across multiple vendors, we identified recurring architectural weaknesses affecting user device trust, communication security, sensor management functionality, and backend authorization controls. Guided by a comprehensive threat model, we analyzed the design and implementation decisions behind these platforms, focusing on wireless communications, trust establishment, authentication, and the broader security architecture of modern CGM ecosystems. This methodology enabled us to identify recurring weaknesses that span multiple vendors rather than isolated implementation flaws. In this Briefing, we will demonstrate how attackers in close proximity can exploit weaknesses in device pairing and trust establishment to impersonate trusted devices, why protocol obscurity at the wireless layer fails as a security boundary, and what manufacturers must change to build more resilient CGM ecosystems. Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of the relevant threat scenarios, the systemic design flaws affecting these devices, and the broader implications that insecure wireless connectivity, weak trust assumptions, and poor security engineering practices have on the safety, privacy, and reliability of modern connected medical technologies. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway An understanding of how commercial glucose monitors actually establish trust across the sensor, phone, and cloud - and where that chain breaks down when pairing is implemented with authentication and secrets that are baked into mobile apps and firmware. Why encrypting glucose traffic in software fails when the same secret lives in both the mobile app and the sensor firmware, and how to find that design flaw in other body-worn health products before it ships. How weak wireless pairing on the sensor can lead to serious issues: stolen live readings, tampered calibration values, and cloud APIs that return another patient's glucose history - and what other vendors did differently to anchor trust from the start.

sessions.title: ON-DEMAND - pwno-code: Breaking Isolation in 10 No-Code & AI Agent Platforms
sessions.abstract: ON-DEMAND - pwno-code: Breaking Isolation in 10 No-Code & AI Agent Platforms AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Shai Dvash | Security Researcher, Palo Alto Networks Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cloud Security, AI & ML: Attack and Defense Vault Recording: TBD No-code, AI automation, and agentic platforms are rapidly gaining popularity, enabling even non-technical users to build and deploy AI-powered workflows and agents. To provide this flexibility, these platforms often expose server-side code execution and HTTP request modules as core product functionality. In practice, these become attacker-controlled execution and network primitives, enabling sandbox escapes, cross-tenant compromise, cloud takeover, and even direct theft of funds from AI agents' crypto wallets. In this Briefing, I present an offensive study of no-code and agent-automation platforms including Make.com (400k customers, 2nd in no-code market), Virtuals.io (~$350M crypto AI-agent economy platform), Fetch.ai (~$380M decentralized AI-agent ecosystem), Activepieces, ToolJet, MindStudio, Windmill, Latenode, Albato and BuildShip. This study uncovered more than 15 vulnerabilities (12 Critical, 6 High) across ten platforms, spanning five vulnerability categories: sandbox escapes, cross-tenant data exposure, cloud infrastructure compromise, server-side request abuse, and AI-agent asset theft. I will walk through representative demos from each category. This Briefing is not a bug parade. It is a category study of how code-execution-as-a-service platforms fail, why those failures keep recurring, and how to audit and mitigate them efficiently. I will walk through recurring exploitation patterns and show representative case studies from ten vendors, ranging from unauthenticated RCE and cross-tenant secret IDORs to complete platform compromise via ECR overwrite. These will be distilled into a reusable assessment methodology for researchers and a concrete hardening checklist for defenders. As these systems move into production at scale, this briefing takes a deliberately offensive approach to their security boundaries and failure modes. Through deep dives into real-world exploitation chains, I will show how seemingly isolated primitives can be chained into full platform compromise, cross-tenant access, cloud infrastructure takeover, and AI-agent asset theft. The focus is on the attacker's perspective: identifying the exposed primitives, breaking isolation boundaries, chaining vulnerabilities, and turning individual weaknesses into practical paths to compromise. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Understand the attack surface of no-code and cloud agentic platforms - how their architecture, code-execution capabilities, HTTP primitives, secrets, and cloud integrations create opportunities for attackers to break isolation and pivot across trust boundaries. Learn a reusable offensive methodology for auditing code-execution-as-a-service platforms - from identifying attacker-controlled primitives and isolation boundaries to discovering vulnerabilities, chaining weaknesses, and turning individual primitives into practical compromise paths. Analyze real-world exploitation chains and their impact - including sandbox escapes, cross-tenant access, cloud infrastructure compromise, SSRF, secret theft, and AI-agent asset theft, with a focus on how seemingly isolated flaws can be chained into full compromise.

sessions.title: ON-DEMAND - Too Close to the Metal: Cross-Tenant Attacks in GPU Neo-Clouds
sessions.abstract: ON-DEMAND - Too Close to the Metal: Cross-Tenant Attacks in GPU Neo-Clouds AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Yakir Kadkoda | CTO, Lava Michael Katchinskiy | Head of Security Research, Lava Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Platform Security, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD AI did not just create new models. It created a new kind of cloud: GPU neo-clouds. Neo-clouds let anyone rent high-end, often bare-metal GPU infrastructure in minutes. They look like hyperscalers from the customer side, but their security boundaries are newer, thinner, and closer to the underlying infrastructure. This Briefing presents cross-tenant vulnerabilities and design flaws found across multiple neo-cloud providers using only standard customer access. The findings span the layers that make neo-clouds different from traditional cloud: backend accelerator fabrics, shared storage systems, bare-metal hosts, and out-of-band management paths. In one class of issues, we were able to mount filesystems belonging to other tenants. In another, exposed InfiniBand fabric controls allowed us to map the backend network, observe GPU-related fabric traffic, and influence traffic flow through the fabric. In a third scenario, we show how a tenant on a bare-metal host could reach the server's own BMC through an unauthenticated interface, crossing toward the management network customers are never meant to reach. Rather than treating GPU neo-clouds as traditional clouds with expensive GPUs, this talk examines what changes when tenants rent bare-metal servers inside newer infrastructure built around AI-scale GPU clusters. We conclude with a tenant-side methodology, assessment tool, and checklist for evaluating overlooked layers of GPU neo-cloud security before running sensitive workloads. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17 - January 29. Takeaway Understand the GPU neo-cloud attack surface. Attendees will learn how security issues appear in AI infrastructure layers that are rarely discussed in traditional cloud security, including accelerator fabrics such as InfiniBand and RoCE, GPU-related systems, shared storage, bare-metal hosts, and out-of-band management planes. In mature hyperscalers, many of these layers are heavily abstracted away from tenants. In GPU neo-clouds, tenants may be much closer to them. Attendees will see how tenant isolation can break down beneath the operating system and cloud API, including cases where a tenant can observe, influence, or reach infrastructure that should have remained isolated. Assess a GPU neo-cloud from the customer side. Attendees will learn how to safely evaluate a rented GPU environment from a normal tenant position and use our assessment tool to identify risky exposure before running sensitive workloads. Harden the infrastructure behind GPU workloads. Attendees who operate AI clusters, GPU clouds, or data center environments will learn which backend controls to validate, including fabric isolation, storage authorization, management-plane scoping, admin access paths, cleanup workflows, and evidence that tenant isolation actually works.

sessions.title: ON-DEMAND - Too Many Findings, Not Enough Meaning: Building an AWS-Native Security Graph for Permission Governance, Boundary Detection, and Threat Containment
sessions.abstract: ON-DEMAND - Too Many Findings, Not Enough Meaning: Building an AWS-Native Security Graph for Permission Governance, Boundary Detection, and Threat Containment AVAILABLE 17 DECEMBER IN THE MOBILE APP ON-DEMAND ONLY Chandler Niu | Security Researcher, Bitget Security Lab Jesse Cao | Security Expert, Bitget Security Lab Aaron | Security Director, Bitget Security Lab Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 22:30-23:00  ( On-Demand ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Defense & Resilience, Cloud Security Vault Recording: TBD Your AWS environment changed again overnight. IAM roles gained or retained access to thousands of resources, test accounts acquired new network paths into protected workloads, Inspector reported vulnerable assets, and GuardDuty raised suspicious-activity findings. Which of these signals represents real business risk—and which Security Group, IAM permission, or AWS relationship should defenders change first? Most cloud security tools answer only one part of that question. Static IAM analysis shows what a role can do, but not how those permissions are used on each connected resource. CloudTrail shows observed activity, but not whether an unusual permission reaches a critical business asset. Raw graph diff reports every changed edge, but not whether hundreds of edges represent one boundary failure. Inspector and GuardDuty identify local asset risk, but do not explain the downstream network, identity, and business impact. In this Briefing, we will show how we built an AWS-native security graph that combines network reachability, IAM permissions, CloudTrail behavior, AWS-native security findings, business context, and root-cause evidence. In a recent enterprise snapshot, the graph contained 61,330 active nodes and more than 5.9 million security-relevant relationships, including 4.32 million network edges and 1.61 million permission edges. We will present two relationship-level permission analyses using 30 days of CloudTrail activity for 238 IAM roles associated with business-critical assets. The first compares configured and observed actions for each role-to-resource relationship to identify least-privilege review candidates. The second derives dominant permission patterns across groups of similar adjacent resources and identifies individual configuration outliers. The resulting report surfaced findings for 97 roles. Permission-convergence analysis compressed 37,483 adjacent relationships into 137 reviewable findings, while peer analysis identified isolated exceptions inside resource groups containing as many as 3,761 neighbors. Unobserved actions are treated as evidence for review—not as instructions for automatic removal. We will also show how risk-adaptive aggregation converts network change into operational boundary events. In one cross-snapshot analysis, the system identified 1,670 newly added test-to-non-test network edges. Rather than generating 1,670 alerts, it preserved the edges as evidence and compressed them into 29 events: 28 destination-centric alerts involving business-critical assets or protected VPCs, and one account-pair summary. In one case, 92 new edges from two test accounts converged on a single critical EC2 workload and became one actionable alert tied to the Security Groups responsible for the access. Finally, we will explain how the graph incorporates AWS-native exposure features, Inspector vulnerability evidence, and GuardDuty threat evidence to create explainable risk states. Inspector tells us what may be exploitable. GuardDuty tells us what may already be happening. The graph tells us what the affected asset can reach, why it matters to the business, and which AWS control can contain it. Attendees will leave with practical algorithms and design patterns for turning millions of AWS relationships into a small number of explainable permission findings, business-boundary events, and defensive decisions. Briefing is available On-Demand only to Briefings Pass Holders via the Black Hat Events App, December 17

sessions.title: Phantom Bytes: A Complete Taxonomy of Linux Memory Attacks Against Modern EDR
sessions.abstract: Phantom Bytes: A Complete Taxonomy of Linux Memory Attacks Against Modern EDR ShuFeng Yi | Senior Security Researcher, Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. Yuan Zhang | Security Researcher, Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Track : Malware Vault Recording: TBD In January 2026, researchers disclosed VoidLink, a sophisticated Linux malware framework targeting cloud environments. Its capabilities were alarming: it used `memfd_create` with `execveat` to execute payloads entirely from memory, masqueraded as a kernel worker thread, profiled and evaded endpoint security products in real time, and relied on server-side compilation, where its C2 dynamically built kernel modules for each victim's kernel version. This was not isolated; around the same time, multiple research teams reported similar Linux fileless, memory-resident malware families, showing that these techniques are already being used in the wild. The security industry has become effective at detecting Windows memory attacks such as process hollowing, DLL stomping, and reflective loading. Linux, however, remains far less systematically understood. Its kernel exposes memory-manipulation primitives with no direct Windows equivalent: cross-process file descriptor theft, secret anonymous memory, memory remapping, and post-execution page-table cleanup. These Linux-native capabilities remain weakly monitored by many endpoint products, giving attackers new paths to evade detection. This Briefing presents a systematic map of Linux memory attacks across three evasion domains. For each technique, we explain how it works, demonstrate its impact, and provide practical detection strategies defenders can implement. Several techniques discussed in this talk have not been publicly documented before, including a memory parasite that hides inside a whitelisted system binary using only two syscalls and a shellcode relay that fragments payloads across secret memory so the full code is never contiguous. Our goal is simple: give defenders a practical framework to understand, detect, and respond to Linux memory-resident threats before they scale. VoidLink shows what is already happening; this talk shows what may come next — and how to defend against it. Takeaway A systematic crash course on Linux fileless and memory-resident attack techniques, organizing previously fragmented knowledge into a clear framework for understanding execution, hiding, evasion, and cleanup primitives. Concrete methods to detect advanced Linux memory attacks through kernel-level syscall tracing, cross-process correlation, and targeted memory inspection. A GitHub repository with research PoCs and detection code, including previously undocumented Linux memory attack techniques and ready-to-implement defensive logic for Linux EDR and incident response teams.

sessions.title: Playing with AI Data Collection Bots for Fun and Profit
sessions.abstract: Playing with AI Data Collection Bots for Fun and Profit Nethanel Gelernter | CEO, Atom41 Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : AI & ML: Attack and Defense, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD Data fuels AI. In the LLM race, the players make significant efforts to collect data that will give them an advantage. While Google (Gemini) comes with a well-established data collection system, the other giant players, most-notably Anthropic and OpenAI (on which this research is focused), need to close the gap, and they do so aggressively. In this Briefing, we will present the first systematic security analysis of AI data collection bots. We first "reverse-engineer" the proactive web data collection mechanisms of the big AI players through 50+ experiments over 9 weeks, analyzing 20M+ bot requests. We then demonstrate three novel attack classes that exploit these bots' behavior: (1) Amplification-based Denial-of-Service achieving 100K+ amplification factor, using a new metric we introduce the response:request-response ratio, which inverts the traditional amplification model: the attacker's single HTTP response triggers massive outbound traffic, rather than a crafted request. (2) Denial-of-Wallet attacks that drain hundreds of dollars of a target's cloud budget from a single HTTP response. (3) Weaponizing AI bots as Out-of-Band attack proxies to deliver payloads such as log4shell and blind XSS at scale, including a technique to bypass robots.txt restrictions via certificate mismatch exploitation. All attacks operate under an extremely weak attacker model: no vulnerabilities need to be exploited on the target (for DoS/DoW), no special access or capabilities are required, and the entire attack infrastructure costs a $1 domain and a $3/month VPS. The attacker simply serves web pages, and the AI data collection bots do the rest. We have shared our research and findings with the relevant AI players to mitigate the issues on their side. Anthropic confirmed and fixed the reported issues, and we wait for a fix from others. In the meantime, we publish the scripts that allow teams to reproduce the research and test whether their sites could be targeted, and provide clear defense recommendations. Takeaway AI players: Collecting data at scale - consider potential abuse and handle it. Limit by size (for the ones that do not do this yet), don't follow insecure hyperlinks (that by nature could be abused) or ones that your WAF would be blocking, and be less aggressive (Luckily, at least Anthropic already applied these takeaways; others will follow) Red-team/pentesters: Beyond tools that allow to reproduce the attacks and check whether targets could be abused (as long as some AI players don't fix): If sites are not correctly verifying SNI/host headers and robots.txt is not used - they are exposed to no/low cost attack via AI data collection infrastructure. Simulate such a minimal attack (bonus - find the largest resource you can abuse) Search for S3 like resources that could be abused for denial of money. Apply this especially on storage/static assets with large resources, that are usually ignored as they are considered to be of a lower priority (compared to dynamic content or the main apps). Blue-team: Beyond tools that allow to reproduce the attacks and check whether targets could be abused (as long as some AI players don't fix): Robots.txt and server configuration (e.g., Nginx) should consider traffic and either block it or limit it. Add robots.txt files also to storage/static domains if you don't want static resources to be abused for denial-of-wallet/service.

sessions.title: Reconstructing a Ransomware Organization from Underground Breadcrumbs: Mapping the Hidden Business Ecosystem of Modern Cybercrime
sessions.abstract: Reconstructing a Ransomware Organization from Underground Breadcrumbs: Mapping the Hidden Business Ecosystem of Modern Cybercrime Assaf Morag | Security Researcher, Flare Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Threat Hunting & Incident Response, Enterprise Security Vault Recording: TBD For years, defenders have analyzed ransomware through malware samples, leaked chats, infrastructure, and victim reports. While these approaches reveal how attacks occur, they rarely explain how ransomware organizations actually function as businesses. This research reconstructs the operational architecture of a modern ransomware enterprise by analyzing years of underground activity across dozens of criminal forums, messaging platforms, and marketplaces. Rather than focusing on malware, we developed an identity-centric methodology that pivots on durable underground identifiers—including qTox IDs, Jabber accounts, XMPP identities, Telegram handles, Session IDs, and long-term behavioral patterns—to attribute relationships between actors with high confidence. Using this methodology, we reconstructed a complete ransomware supply chain consisting of initial access brokers, ransomware developers, affiliate operators, access sellers, cryptocurrency monetization services, fake ransomware recovery companies, and supporting infrastructure. The resulting graph exposes how independent criminal services cooperate to operate as a coordinated business rather than as isolated threat actors. The Briefing demonstrates how these relationships evolved over nearly a decade, how criminal specialization mirrors legitimate software supply chains, and how defenders can identify emerging ransomware ecosystems before large-scale campaigns become publicly visible. Rather than presenting another ransomware case study, this Briefing introduces a repeatable investigative methodology for mapping criminal organizations and understanding the hidden economics that enable modern ransomware operations. Takeaway Recognize the specialized business roles that compose modern ransomware ecosystems, including access brokers, developers, affiliates, monetization services, and supporting criminal infrastructure. Observe the evolution of ransomware groups across 10+ years of activity, based on underground advertisements, recruitments, comments, and offerings. Apply an identity-based methodology to reconstruct relationships between underground actors using persistent communication identifiers rather than malware artifacts alone. Build higher-confidence threat intelligence by combining long-term behavioral analysis with underground identity pivots to identify emerging ransomware operations earlier.

sessions.title: Render Safe: Reverse Engineering the PackBot and FirstLook Tactical Robotics Ecosystem
sessions.abstract: Render Safe: Reverse Engineering the PackBot and FirstLook Tactical Robotics Ecosystem Patrick Kiley | Principal Red Team Consultant, Google/Mandiant Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT, Reverse Engineering Vault Recording: TBD Remotely operated systems are increasingly integral to modern operations, with explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) robots serving as some of the earliest pioneers of deployed robotics. This Briefing provides a deep technical analysis into the architecture, attack surface, and 25-year evolution of iRobot's PackBot. Originally developed by iRobot, creators of the Roomba vacuum, the PackBot saw extensive use since its creation. However, beneath its ruggedized exterior lies a fragile ecosystem built on legacy open-source software, commercial off-the-shelf hardware, and significant technical debt. Despite two decades of iterative hardware improvements, the PackBot's software stack has remained largely static, running on legacy Linux distributions and relying heavily on Python 2.5 for core functionality in its second-generation and later models. Given its critical use case in the field, this technical debt has resulted in potentially dangerous, systemic security vulnerabilities. Attendees will be taken through a comprehensive hardware teardown and software deep dive of the Intel-based PackBot platform, alongside its throwable counterpart, the ARM-based FirstLook. We will map the attack surface across the Operator Control Units, the radio links, and the shared Aware2 software ecosystem. Finally, we will detail recently disclosed vulnerabilities across these platforms, covering a critical unauthenticated Local File Inclusion (LFI), and several others that when chained together, leave both robots vulnerable to total compromise. Takeaway Security by Obscurity is a Failed Strategy - Attendees will learn why relying on physical isolation and proprietary connectors is not a substitute for standard security practices. They will walk away with actionable insights into why hardware-level trust boundaries and defense-in-depth are mandatory, even for physically restricted or air-gapped tactical systems Methodologies for Auditing Robotics and IoT Command and Control (C2) - The audience will learn practical, hands-on techniques for reverse-engineering undocumented hardware and control protocols. Attendees will leave this talk knowing how to approach custom communication links, intercept telemetry streams, and map out discovery and control architectures in proprietary embedded devices to uncover high-impact vulnerabilities The Cascading Risk of Legacy Technical Debt - Using open-source software accelerates development but introduces severe risks if an upgrade path is not maintained. Attendees will see the real-world impact of stagnant tech stacks (like Python 2.5, unencrypted WiFi, and 15-year-old Linux kernels) in long-lifecycle devices. They will also learn strategies for identifying and retrofitting security into unpatchable legacy ecosystems

sessions.title: Rooting Your Robots: Breaking Authentication Across Quadruped and Humanoid Robots
sessions.abstract: Rooting Your Robots: Breaking Authentication Across Quadruped and Humanoid Robots Yuqiao Yang | PhD Student, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Fuchen Ma | Postdoctoral Researcher, Tsinghua University Ting Chen | Professor, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Yu Jiang | Professor, Tsinghua University Yuanyuan Yuan | Assistant Professor, Tsinghua University Yuanming Xie | Master Student, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Minglang Li | Undergraduate Student, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Xinnuo Ying | Master Student, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China Ao Wang | Research Intern, Tsinghua University Jiaxin Dong | Research Intern, Tsinghua University Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Track : Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT Vault Recording: TBD Legged robots, quadrupeds and humanoids alike have achieved mass deployment across homes, offices, and industrial facilities. Unitree commands nearly 70% of the global market share. DeepRobotics holds the #2 position worldwide with over 85% market share in power grid inspection. Agibot stands as one of the most prominent Chinese humanoid robotics companies. Xiaomi CyberDog stands as one of the most representative open quadruped platforms. We selected representative flagship models from these four major platforms for our analysis. Together, these four platforms span open platforms to commercial to industrial tiers. They share one catastrophic commonality: their authentication architectures are either absent by design or shattered by implementation. The authentication designs of commercial legged robots have never been systematically studied. We will present the first such analysis, modeling the human-robot trust lifecycle across three phases: device discovery, identity authentication, and post-authentication operation, and systematically auditing the full attack surface of the four platforms. The findings are devastating: every phase, every platform, authentication is either missing by design or broken by implementation, with bypass achievable in all cases. We identify a novel vulnerability class: Physiological Motion Vulnerabilities. Without injecting malicious code, an attacker can weaponize legitimate motion primitives by orchestrating physiologically anomalous action sequences, driving the robot to execute unexpected, undefined dangerous motions, self-destructive leaps and falls, transforming "normal movement" into targeted physical destruction, and even bodily harm to humans. Building on these findings, we design and demonstrate three end-to-end attacks: • Full Body Takeover: Unauthorized complete control of locomotion and sensory systems • Sensory Hijacking: Covert activation of cameras for physical space surveillance • Physiological Destruction: Device self-damage via malicious motion choreography All attacks are executable without authorization and without physical access. We have responsibly disclosed all vulnerabilities to affected vendors. Takeaway A reusable three-phase framework (discovery → authentication → post-auth operation) that attendees can apply to audit authentication in other robot or cyber-physical systems, not just legged robots. Concrete implementation-level patterns that break "secure-looking" designs in practice, such as hardcoded keys in binaries, shared certificates across all units, and no-op authorization functions, so attendees know exactly what to look for during their own reviews. Evidence that current robot controllers have no biomechanical safety envelope: we forced commercial quadrupeds into gait-and-motion combinations no real dog could physically perform (e.g., synchronized ipsilateral leg movement combined with a sharp turn), and every one of these physically impossible commands was accepted and executed as valid. Attendees will learn to test command sequences against real animal biomechanic

sessions.title: Sight Unseen: Exploiting TCL RayNeo X3 Pro Android AR Smart Glasses "Vulnerable Out of the Box"
sessions.abstract: Sight Unseen: Exploiting TCL RayNeo X3 Pro Android AR Smart Glasses "Vulnerable Out of the Box" Edward (Actuator) Warren | Principle Security Researcher Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Mobile, Hardware / Embedded Vault Recording: TBD Modern Android XR devices rely heavily on pre-installed OEM applications that operate with elevated privileges. This Briefing presents original research into application-security failures on the TCL RayNeo X3 Pro Smart AR Glasses. I demonstrate how exposed inter-process communication (IPC) interfaces in system-privileged components can be abused from a zero-permission third-party application, progressively undermining Android's permission model. The research shows a structured escalation across confidentiality, integrity, and authority boundaries: (1) delegated access to protected GPS data without location permissions, (2) delegated execution of privileged telephony actions without CALL_PHONE permission, and (3) silent granting of dangerous runtime permissions with no user consent. In parallel, additional vulnerability classes are identified in vendor components, including arbitrary file write via path traversal and heap out-of-bounds conditions reachable in native libraries. These findings illustrate a broader class of issues where OEM applications redefine trust boundaries through insecure IPC design, insufficient caller validation, and unsafe exposure of privileged functionality. System components effectively become confused deputies. These failures occur on a device that has no Play Store and no Play Integrity attestation. While Google continues to tighten developer verification and installation restrictions, the highest-privilege code on this platform never goes through those controls. Takeaway Attendees will learn practical techniques to identify and exploit insecure IPC surfaces and vendor component flaws in privileged Android/OEM apps, applicable to mobile, IoT, and XR devices. They will gain a structured understanding of how zero-permission apps can escalate across security boundaries via confused deputy attacks, enabling them to test similar assumptions in their own research or assessments. Practical defensive strategies will be shared, including treating IPC as a first-class security boundary, enforcing caller validation, and reducing attack surface in pre-installed components, which is actionable for developers, vendors, and researchers.

sessions.title: SIPConfusion: Exploiting SIP Semantic Ambiguities for Caller ID and SMS Spoofing
sessions.abstract: SIPConfusion: Exploiting SIP Semantic Ambiguities for Caller ID and SMS Spoofing Jianjun Chen | Associate Professor, Tsinghua University Jingcheng Yang | Ph.D Student, Tsinghua University Jiahe Zhang | Ph.D Student, Tsinghua University Yaru Yang | Ph.D Student, Tsinghua University Haixin Duan | Professor, Tsinghua University Eki | Ph.D. Student, Tsinghua University / Baidu Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Network Security, Mobile Vault Recording: TBD SIP—the signaling backbone of VoIP, VoLTE, and RCS—is deployed across billions of devices and carrier networks. Yet despite two decades of standardization, SIP remains fragmented and overly flexible. This flexibility has created a minefield of subtle, cross-implementation semantic ambiguities — an attack surface we define as SIPConfusion. In this Briefing, we will introduce SIPCHIMERA, a new grammar-aware black-box fuzzing framework, and present the first large-scale security analysis of SIPConfusion. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked and systemic attack surface in modern telecommunications infrastructure, showing that SIP identity spoofing is far from solved—and that semantic inconsistencies across vendors represent a new foundational class of vulnerabilities enabling telecom fraud and impersonation at scale. We will demonstrate live exploits, real-world case studies, and validated proof-of-concept attacks across popular VoIP deployments and multiple RCS operators collectively serving over a billion users. We will also release SIPCHIMERA as an open-source framework capable of systematically uncovering ambiguity-driven vulnerabilities in SIP and other text-based protocols. Takeaway Discover a new root-cause class behind persistent caller ID and SMS spoofing: semantic inconsistencies between SIP servers, phone clients, VoIP devices, and RCS infrastructures Understand why spoofing succeeds even when authentication is enforced Explore how our work exposes systemic flaws in SIP parsing, trust decisions, and header precedence that attackers can exploit to impersonate any user.

sessions.title: Taking Over GitHub.com: RCE on GitHub With a Single Git Push
sessions.abstract: Taking Over GitHub.com: RCE on GitHub With a Single Git Push Sagi Tzadik | Security Researcher, Wiz (Google) Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Cloud Security, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD We achieved remote code execution on GitHub.com - the world's largest code hosting platform - using nothing but a standard git push command. By exploiting a fundamental injection flaw we discovered in how GitHub's internal services process a push (CVE-2026-3854), any user could execute arbitrary commands on GitHub's backend infrastructure, breaking tenant isolation and exposing millions of private repositories belonging to other organizations and users. GitHub's git pipeline passes user-controlled data through a chain of internal services, each written in a different language, each parsing that data in its own way. We suspected the boundaries between them could hide vulnerabilities invisible to any single-component audit. Testing this against GitHub.com directly would be blind - but GitHub Enterprise Server ships as a self-hosted appliance with the same pipeline binaries. AI-augmented reverse engineering gave us the visibility we needed, and what we found proved us right. In this Briefing, we will walk through the full attack chain: from reverse engineering GHES binaries to discovering the injection primitive, escalating to RCE by chaining overrides, and adapting the exploit from a self-hosted appliance to GitHub.com's multi-tenant production infrastructure. We will demonstrate the attack, discuss the broader implications for any architecture that passes user-controlled data through shared internal protocols, and share how AI-augmented tooling is changing the economics of vulnerability research. Takeaway Multi-service architectures that pass user-controlled data through shared internal protocols are a systemic risk. Attendees will gain practical insight into how to audit their own internal protocol designs for similar systemic problems. AI-augmented reverse engineering tools are fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability research. Attendees will see firsthand how these tools enabled rapid analysis of large compiled binaries and protocol reconstruction, and will understand how to incorporate these tools into their own offensive and defensive workflows. Attendees will learn a concrete, novel attack technique and understand how parser differentials between services written in different languages can be exploited to override security-critical internal metadata, bypass sandboxes, and achieve remote code execution.

sessions.title: The Black Hat Europe Network Operations Center (NOC) Report
sessions.abstract: The Black Hat Europe Network Operations Center (NOC) Report Neil (Grifter) Wyler | Vice President of Defensive Services, Coalfire Bart Stump | Managing Principal, Coalfire Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 16:20-17:00  ( George V Room 1 & 2, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Network Security, Application Security: Defense Vault Recording: TBD Back with another year of soul-crushing statistics, the Black Hat NOC team will be sharing all of the data that keeps us equally puzzled, and entertained, year after year. We'll let you know all the tools and techniques we're using to set up, stabilize, and secure the network, and what changes we've made over the past year to try and keep doing things better. Of course, we'll be sharing some of the more humorous network activity and what it helps us learn about the way security professionals conduct themselves on an open WiFi network. Takeaway Insight into the tools and techniques behind securing a high-stakes, high-traffic network. Real-world data on how security professionals behave on open WiFi. Lessons for improving your own network security practices.

sessions.title: The Core Was Suppressed, the Uncore Was Not: Leaking Intel Confidential Computing Secrets from Outside the Core
sessions.abstract: The Core Was Suppressed, the Uncore Was Not: Leaking Intel Confidential Computing Secrets from Outside the Core Decheng Chen | Ph.D. Student, South China University of Technology Zhi Zhang | Senior Lecturer, The University of Western Australia Zhenkai Zhang | Assistant Professor, Clemson University Xin Zhang | Associate Professor, Shandong University Yansong Gao | Professor, Southeast University Yi Zou | Professor, South China University of Technology Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 15:20-16:00  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Hardware / Embedded, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD For years, a reassuring assumption has shaped Intel confidential computing: once execution enters a protected domain such as SGX or TDX, performance monitoring is suppressed to close Performance Monitoring Counter(PMC)-based side channels. This Briefing overturns that assumption. The suppression is enforced inside the CPU core, but modern Xeon processors are not just cores. They are full systems-on-chip, with shared uncore components such as mesh fabrics and memory controllers. For the first time, we will expose this whole-chip blind spot in Intel's confidential-computing stack. We will show that while core performance monitoring is effectively suppressed during protected execution, uncore performance monitoring remains active. We identify and reverse engineer a mesh-to-memory event that turns this overlooked hardware observability into UncoreBleed, a practical side-channel primitive against Intel SGX and TDX: while a protected workload is running, the uncore quietly leaks its memory behaviors at 64-B granularity. Importantly, UncoreBleed does not trigger any page fault or interrupt, thus creating no asynchronous enclave exit (AEX). This is why it bypasses Intel AEX-Notify, the latest SGX side-channel hardening on recent Xeon processors, and TLBlur, the off-the-shelf SGX software defense built on top of it. Both expect attacks to leave an AEX-visible footprint, while UncoreBleed leaves none. We weaponize UncoreBleed against SGX in two end-to-end attacks on Xeon platforms: recovering JPEG images from a Libjpeg enclave and extracting RSA private keys from an enclaved RSA engine. We further validate UncoreBleed against Intel TDX, showing that the same uncore monitoring primitive remains feasible against running Trust Domains. The broader lesson is that Intel confidential computing cannot be secured by core-level hardening alone. If the uncore can still watch protected execution, system-wide hardening must treat the whole chip as the trusted boundary. Takeaway Intel confidential computing does not fully suppress performance monitoring. Attendees will learn how our attacks overturn the long-held assumption that Intel confidential computing suppresses performance monitoring enough to close PMC-based side channels: the core goes silent, but the uncore keeps observing protected execution. The uncore hides a practical side-channel primitive. We will walk through how we reverse engineered an event in the mesh-to-memory subsystem, recovered its filtering semantics, undocumented event codes, and address-to-M2M mappings, and turned it into 64-byte monitoring of selected protected memory accesses across multiple Xeon generations. UncoreBleed is an AEX-free side channel that breaks the latest defense model. Attendees will see how UncoreBleed becomes the first PMC-based side channel against SGX, bypassing Intel's latest SGX side-channel hardening and off-the-shelf SGX software defense. We will also show why UncoreBleed remains feasible against TDX, motivating uncore-level mitigations as a necessary part of Intel confidential-computing security.

sessions.title: The Vulnerabilities You Already Know, in Files You Never Audit: Exploiting GitHub Actions at Scale
sessions.abstract: The Vulnerabilities You Already Know, in Files You Never Audit: Exploiting GitHub Actions at Scale Elad Meged | Founding Team Security Researcher, Novee Security Omri Inbar | Founding Team Security Researcher, Novee Security Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Defense, Application Security: Offense Vault Recording: TBD GitHub Actions workflows hold signing keys, authenticate to cloud providers, and publish releases. The same vulnerability classes security teams track in application code - command injection, broken authorization, privilege escalation - exist in these workflow files, but no mainstream security tool audits them as code. We scanned 30,000 open-source repositories across the npm, PyPI, crates, and Go ecosystems and confirmed over 300 fully exploitable chains, including at Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Apache, WordPress, Cloudflare, and the Python Software Foundation. A pull request comment steals a non-expiring GitHub App key from Microsoft Sentinel. A fork PR escalates through two workflows to GCP roles/owner on a Google Cloud project. Two zero-click paths give full write access to an Apache database used by 10,000+ enterprises. All responsibly disclosed and vendor-confirmed. The most dangerous findings are cross-workflow compositions: untrusted data from a low-privilege workflow flows into a high-privilege workflow through artifacts or workflow_run triggers. Neither workflow is vulnerable alone. The exploit exists only in how they connect - a class no existing scanner or linter detects. We present a taxonomy mapping each class to its application-security equivalent, the AI-agent methodology that discovered these compositions at scale, and a practitioner framework for auditing CI/CD trust boundaries. Takeaway A taxonomy of five CI/CD workflow vulnerability classes mapped from application security to GitHub Actions YAML - command injection, code injection, broken authorization, artifact poisoning, and cross-workflow privilege escalation - with concrete exploitation patterns for each. A repeatable audit methodology for cross-workflow trust boundaries: tracing untrusted input from a pull request or comment through artifact handoffs, environment variables, and workflow_run triggers into privileged execution contexts. How AI agents discover cross-workflow composition bugs that static analysis structurally cannot detect, and why AI coding agents are reproducing the same insecure patterns across new repositories.

sessions.title: Uncovering Fraud in Africa's Biggest Welfare System
sessions.abstract: Uncovering Fraud in Africa's Biggest Welfare System Veer Gosai | Security Research Unit Lead, Nascent Group Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 13:30-14:10  ( Victoria 6, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Policy, Humans Factors Vault Recording: TBD After turning 18, I discovered that someone had used my identity to claim South Africa's Social Relief of Distress grant. What began as a personal case of identity fraud led me to uncover something far bigger. An API weakness in the public application portal allowed me to test national ID numbers, revealing that fraudulent grant applications were being submitted at a systematic scale. This Briefing follows how I turned one suspicious application into a national investigation, validated the pattern, responsibly disclosed findings and ultimately presented the evidence before South Africa's Parliament. I will break down missing rate limits, weak identity verification and failures that left victims with no way to recover. This is the story of how one overlooked API exposed serious weaknesses in a welfare system relied upon by millions of South Africa's Poorest Individuals, all for a R350 (21$ / 17£) welfare grant for unemployed people. Takeaway Test API impact at population scale - Attendees will learn how to move beyond assessing the sensitivity of a single API response and test whether enumeration, predictable identifiers, missing authentication and weak rate limiting allow a harmless-looking endpoint to become a population-scale abuse mechanism. Turn application data into defensible fraud intelligence - Attendees will learn a repeatable method for defining an expected baseline, dividing applicants into meaningful cohorts, comparing observed and expected distributions, validating anomalies against external demographic data and communicating the difference between suspicious patterns and confirmed fraud. Build identity verification that resists fraud without excluding users - Attendees will leave with a layered verification model combining facial matching, liveness, bank-account ownership, device and network intelligence, behavioural signals, step-up checks and accessible recovery paths. They will be able to test whether a control stops fraudsters without also blocking legitimate users with old identity photographs, low-cost phones or unreliable internet access.

sessions.title: Unlocking Cars in 2026: Reconstructing Firmwares Through RF Reverse Engineering
sessions.abstract: Unlocking Cars in 2026: Reconstructing Firmwares Through RF Reverse Engineering Danilo (revers3everything) Erazo | Automotive Security Researcher, PCA Cybersecurity Date : 9 Dec 2026 | 14:30-15:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 30-Minute Briefings Tracks : Reverse Engineering, Cyber-Physical Systems & IoT Vault Recording: TBD Modern Remote Keyless Entry Systems (RKES) continue to rely on proprietary RF protocols and third party components that are often treated as black boxes. Following my 2024 - 2025 research, which resulted in two CVEs (CVSS 9.4) affecting KIA vehicles in Ecuador (2022–2025) and enabled vehicle unlocking without user interaction, KIA's Tier 1 supplier commissioned a security assessment of its next generation RKES intended to replace the vulnerable design. During this assessment, I discovered a novel firmware extraction technique that requires no physical access to the ECU, no chip off, and no hardware probing. By combining RF protocol reversing with systematic brute forcing of receiver state transitions, I reconstructed the receiver's decision logic and effectively dumped the firmware through RF interactions alone. Using this approach, I developed a working exploit that successfully unlocked target vehicles and identified vulnerabilities beyond KIA, including a zero day affecting Suzuki. The research ultimately resulted in four new CVEs in 2026, which allow me to unlock cars in the streets. I also applied the same RF reversing methodology to analyze the security of RKES implementations used by Audi, Alfa Romeo, Toyota, and other manufacturers. This Briefing introduces the RF reversing methodology, explains why these vulnerabilities exist, and demonstrates that the root cause is often the widespread use of aftermarket or third party RKES components in official vehicles. The findings show that this is not an isolated vendor issue but a systemic weakness affecting vehicles worldwide. Finally, I discuss the coordinated disclosure process with KIA's Tier 1 supplier, whose decision not to deploy the vulnerable RKES demonstrates the real world security impact of this research. Takeaway Challenge the assumption that rolling codes guarantee security. Attendees will learn why modern rolling code implementations can still be vulnerable due to design and implementation flaws, and how to identify weaknesses in these systems. Attendees will learn a practical methodology for evaluating Remote Keyless Entry Systems using AutoRFKiller, a tool introduced in this presentation. They will see how to execute attacks and determine whether an RKES is vulnerable or not. Attendees will learn a new technique for reconstructing the internal logic of an RKES receiver exclusively through RF interactions, enabling firmware level analysis, vulnerability discovery, and security validation without physically accessing the ECU.

sessions.title: Whose Fingerprint Is It Anyway? Three Bypasses in Windows Hello ESS
sessions.abstract: Whose Fingerprint Is It Anyway? Three Bypasses in Windows Hello ESS Ceri Coburn | Principal Consultant, NetSPI Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 10:20-11:00  ( Victoria 5, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Platform Security, Reverse Engineering Vault Recording: TBD Windows Hello has been well documented in offensive research for the pre ESS design: PIN unwrap, DPAPI-NG chains, TPM sealed key material, and fingerprint/face template substitution. What is not well documented, and what almost every recent Microsoft investment in Windows Hello touches, is **Enhanced Sign-in Security (ESS)**. ESS runs the sensitive parts of Windows Hello inside VBS/VTL1 trustlets (`NgcIso.exe` for containers and keys, `BioIso.exe` for biometrics), moves the sensor SDCP handshake into that boundary, and re partitions container secret handling so that a VTL0 SYSTEM equivalent attacker is not supposed to be able to reach the material Windows Hello protects. This Briefing deconstructs the ESS trustlets and the RPC surface they expose, then walks three separate trust boundary bypasses. The first turned a trustlet debug interface into a decryption oracle for anything the secure side was protecting. The second let any admin level attacker unlock another user's Windows Hello container through its non ESS fallback wrap, without ever touching the victim's account. The third, lets an attacker enrol their own fingerprint under someone else's identity: they swipe their own finger at LogonUI and Windows Hello logs them in as the victim. Come along for the ride and you won't just walk out with slides. You'll get annotated reversing notes for every NgcIso and BioIso RPC the three attacks touch, the exploit PoC dropped, and a fresh build of **Shwmae**, my public Windows Hello credential recovery tool, that finally treats the ESS paths as first class citizens alongside the pre ESS ones it's covered for a while. Takeaway A working mental model of Windows Hello ESS: trustlet boundaries, RPC endpoints, container SecretStore semantics, SecureBio SEK derivation. A methodology for auditing VBS trustlets that expose IDL surfaces to VTL0. What to look for in AAD handling, blob origin markers, nonce provenance. Three specific failure modes in shipping code: `Test` flagged authorisation gaps (CVE-2025-47969), fallback material provisioned by default and wrapped under a service token (another 2025 CVE), and caller supplied identity plus nonce reuse (PrintSwap 2026). Source and reversing notes for follow on research.

sessions.title: WSUSual Suspects
sessions.abstract: WSUSual Suspects Hugo (hugow) Vincent | Security researcher, Synacktiv Guillaume André | Security researcher, Synacktiv Date : 10 Dec 2026 | 11:20-12:00  ( Victoria 4, Level 3 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Offense, Platform Security Vault Recording: TBD When two critical deserialization vulnerabilities hit Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) last year, they looked like textbook source-to-sink flaws. This raised a question: why did standard static analysis (SAST) tools like CodeQL fail to catch them? What began as a quest to understand these tooling blind spots evolved into a deep dive of the WSUS architecture and ultimately led to the discovery of CVE-2026-50444, a critical Elevation of Privilege (EoP) vulnerability. By chaining a novel authentication bypass with this new vulnerability, any low-privileged domain user can elevate their privileges to WSUS Administrator. It is then possible to push malicious updates to any Windows machine enrolled in the WSUS environment, effectively granting total control over the enterprise Windows machines. In this Briefing, we will walk the audience through the complete journey from initial curiosity to full enterprise compromise. We will start by examining one of the recent WSUS CVEs, analyzing the architectural quirks that allow them to evade modern SAST detection. From there, we will unpack the manual code review process that exposed the underlying authentication mapping flaw at the heart of CVE-2026-50444. We will then reveal the "missing link" required for reliable exploitation: a technique bypassing recent Windows authentication reflection mitigations. By leveraging unpatched Unicode spoofing tricks, we will demonstrate how to coerce a WSUS server's machine account and creatively weaponize its own Kerberos authentication to compromise the infrastructure. Finally, we will transition into post-exploitation. We will start with our custom generic tooling, including Kerberos authenticated SOCKS (krbrelayx) and WSUS API manipulation, showing exactly how to forge, approve, and deploy a malicious update payload. We will conclude with an analysis of Microsoft's patches and actionable takeaways for defenders. Takeaway Learn how to chain Unicode DNS spoofing with Kerberos authentication reflection Gain deep insight into WSUS and its authentication mapping mechanics Understand why classical static analysis tools missed recent critical WSUS deserialization bugs and how manual review bridged the gap

sessions.title: (Mis)adventures with Copilot+: Attacking and Exploiting Windows NPU Drivers
sessions.abstract: (Mis)adventures with Copilot+: Attacking and Exploiting Windows NPU Drivers Nicola Stauffer | Student, Zürich University of Applied Sciences ZHAW Gürkan Gür | Senior Lecturer, Zürich University of Applied Sciences ZHAW Date : Friday, April 4 | 10:20am-11:00am  ( Orchid Junior Ballroom 4211/4311 ) Format : 40-Minute Briefings Tracks : Application Security: Offense, Exploit Development & Vulnerability Discovery Vault Recording: TBD In May 2024, Microsoft introduced a new category of PCs designed for AI, called Copilot+ PCs. According to Microsoft, those PCs are starting a new chapter of AI integration on Windows and, thus, personal computing. Each device will have an NPU enabling the device to run Large-Language Models (LLMs) locally. But how exactly were those NPUs integrated into Windows?
